subject: English
title: Maya and Arjun's Magic Marks
hook: Two friends discover the power of tiny marks that change everything we read.

characters.name: Maya
characters.role: curious learner from a school in Delhi

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Maya's classmate who loves writing stories

characters.name: Dadi
characters.role: Maya's grandmother who tells tales

slides.title: Punctuation
slides.storyContext: Maya and Arjun visit Dadi's house after school and find her old diary filled with strange marks.
slides.inSimpleWords: Let's learn the small marks that make sentences clear!

image.alt: Punctuation — Punctuation

slides.title: The Mysterious Marks
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows them her diary: 'Look, children. See these tiny marks? A full stop, a comma, a question mark—they are like musical notes in a song. Without them, words dance everywhere. With them, words dance just right!' Maya and Arjun lean in, amazed.
slides.inSimpleWords: Punctuation marks are like musical notes—they give sentences rhythm and meaning.

image.alt: The Mysterious Marks — Punctuation

slides.title: Why Punctuation Matters: A Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun reads aloud from Dadi's diary: 'Rishab left without money.' Dadi asks, 'What do you think happened?' Arjun shrugs. Dadi points to another line: 'Rishab left. Without money?' And a third: 'Rishab left without money!' 'See?' says Dadi. 'The same words. Different punctuation. Different stories! The first is sad. The second is a question. The third is shocking. Punctuation changes everything.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The same words with different punctuation tell different stories.

slides.title: Why Punctuation Exists: The Big Picture

points.label: What does punctuation do?
points.text: Punctuation marks tell readers when to pause, when to ask, when to get excited, or when a thought is finished.

points.label: Without punctuation:
points.text: Sentences are confusing and hard to understand. Readers do not know where ideas start and stop.

slides.inSimpleWords: Punctuation is the traffic light for reading—it guides our eyes and our understanding.

slides.title: The Full Stop (.)
slides.storyContext: Arjun reads aloud: 'I am going to the market.' 'That's a complete sentence,' says Dadi. 'A full stop tells us it is finished. Now write a sentence without a full stop, and it feels lost.'

points.label: What is a full stop?
points.text: A dot (.) at the end of a sentence that means it is complete.

points.label: When do we use it?
points.text: After statements: 'The sun is bright today.'

example.problem: I went to school today
example.solution: I went to school today.

slides.inSimpleWords: A full stop ends a sentence and shows it is done.

image.alt: The Full Stop (.) — Punctuation

slides.title: Using Full Stops: Story Practice
slides.storyContext: Maya writes in her notebook: 'I went to school. I played with my friends. We ate lunch together. Then I came home.' Dadi reads it and nods. 'Good! Each sentence is complete. Each full stop is a rest, like a musical pause.'

example.problem: Fix this: Rina saw a butterfly it was yellow and blue it flew away
example.solution: Rina saw a butterfly. It was yellow and blue. It flew away.

slides.inSimpleWords: Full stops separate complete thoughts into clear sentences.

slides.title: When We Don't Use Full Stops: Confusion Happens
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries reading a sentence aloud without full stops: 'The boy ran very fast and his friend followed him and they reached the park and they played cricket and had fun and ate ice cream and went home.' Maya interrupts: 'I cannot breathe! Your sentence has no stopping points!' Dadi laughs: 'Exactly! Without full stops, everything runs together like one long thought instead of many clear ideas.'

slides.title: The Question Mark (?)
slides.storyContext: Maya writes, 'Where did you go yesterday' and reads it to Dadi. Dadi shakes her head: 'That sounds like a question, but we cannot hear it without the mark. Add this!' She points to a curved hook with a dot below.

points.label: What is a question mark?
points.text: A mark (?) that shows someone is asking.

points.label: When do we use it?
points.text: At the end of sentences that ask: 'What is your name?'

example.problem: Do you want to play with me
example.solution: Do you want to play with me?

slides.inSimpleWords: A question mark ends a sentence that asks something.

image.alt: The Question Mark (?) — Punctuation

slides.title: Asking Questions: Story Time
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Maya are playing a question game with Dadi. Arjun asks, 'What time do we eat dinner?' Maya asks, 'Can I have a mango?' Dadi asks, 'Did you finish your homework?' Each sentence with a question mark sounds like it is asking. Without the mark, Dadi says, 'People would not know if you are asking or telling.'

example.problem: Make these questions: (1) What is your name (2) How old are you (3) Where do you live
example.solution: (1) What is your name? (2) How old are you? (3) Where do you live?

slides.inSimpleWords: Question marks turn statements into genuine questions that ask for answers.

slides.title: Feeling the Difference: Excitement vs Calm
slides.storyContext: Dadi writes two versions: 'I saw a butterfly.' and 'I saw a butterfly!' Arjun reads the first calmly, the second with excitement in his voice. Maya says, 'That one mark changed how we FEEL when we read it! The exclamation mark makes us excited too!' Dadi nods: 'That is the power of punctuation—it carries our emotions.'

slides.title: The Comma (,)
slides.storyContext: Arjun writes a list of his toys: 'I have a ball a bat a kite and a top.' Dadi says, 'These things need to breathe! Put tiny pauses between them.' She shows him how commas separate items in a list, like beads on a string.

points.label: What is a comma?
points.text: A small curve mark (,) that shows a tiny pause in a sentence.

points.label: When do we use it?
points.text: To separate words in a list: 'I ate rice, dal, and vegetables.' Or before a name: 'Maya, come here.'

example.problem: We saw monkeys parrots and deer at the zoo
example.solution: We saw monkeys, parrots, and deer at the zoo.

slides.inSimpleWords: A comma is a tiny pause that separates things or ideas.

image.alt: The Comma (,) — Punctuation

slides.title: Commas in Lists and Addresses: Practice
slides.storyContext: Maya is writing a thank-you note to her friend. She writes: 'Dear Priya, I loved the gifts you gave me—the book, the pencils, the stickers, and the chocolate.' Dadi checks it and smiles. 'Perfect! Commas help your reader understand what things you received. Without them, it all runs together.'

example.problem: Add commas: I bought apples bananas oranges and grapes from the market
example.solution: I bought apples, bananas, oranges, and grapes from the market.

slides.inSimpleWords: Commas separate items in a list so readers can understand each one clearly.

slides.title: The Comma's Magic: Making Lists Clear
slides.storyContext: Arjun shows Dadi two versions: 'Fruits I like: apples oranges bananas mangoes' versus 'Fruits I like: apples, oranges, bananas, mangoes.' Dadi points: 'Without commas, is it apples and oranges and bananas and mangoes, or something else? With commas, it is crystal clear—four separate fruits!' Arjun shouts: 'The comma is magic!'

slides.title: The Exclamation Mark (!)
slides.storyContext: Maya suddenly shouts, 'Look at that rainbow!' Dadi laughs and says, 'That exclamation mark is like your shout. It shows big feelings—excitement, surprise, or happiness.'

points.label: What is an exclamation mark?
points.text: A mark (!) that shows strong feelings like excitement or surprise.

points.label: When do we use it?
points.text: At the end of sentences with big feelings: 'What a beautiful day!' or 'Watch out!'

example.problem: We won the game
example.solution: We won the game!

slides.inSimpleWords: An exclamation mark shows big feelings like joy or surprise.

image.alt: The Exclamation Mark (!) — Punctuation

slides.title: Exclamation Marks for Emotion: Real Moments
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Maya are telling Dadi about their school day. Arjun shouts, 'We won the cricket match!' Maya adds, 'It was so close! Everyone cheered!' Dadi reads their words and says, 'I can hear your joy in those exclamation marks. They make me feel the excitement too!'

example.problem: Add exclamation marks to show strong feeling: Look out, A snake, Run away fast
example.solution: Look out! A snake! Run away fast!

slides.inSimpleWords: Exclamation marks show when we are excited, scared, surprised, or have big feelings.

slides.title: Inverted Commas ("  ")
slides.storyContext: Arjun writes a story about his friend. 'How do I show when someone speaks?' he asks. Dadi says, 'Use these curved marks. They frame the exact words someone says, like a picture frame around their voice.'

points.label: What are inverted commas?
points.text: Curved marks (" ") that frame the exact words someone speaks.

points.label: When do we use them?
points.text: When someone is speaking: Maya said, "I love to read."

example.problem: Arjun said let us go to the park
example.solution: Arjun said, "Let us go to the park."

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverted commas show the exact words that someone speaks.

image.alt: Inverted Commas ("  ") — Punctuation

slides.title: Writing Dialogue: Characters Speaking
slides.storyContext: Maya writes a story with dialogue. 'The teacher asked, "Who can answer this question?" Ravi said, "I know the answer!" The teacher replied, "Wonderful!"' Dadi reads and praises her. 'See how inverted commas let your reader hear each character's voice?'

example.problem: Add inverted commas: Rani asked where are you going tomorrow
example.solution: Rani asked, "Where are you going tomorrow?"

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverted commas let readers know exactly what someone said word for word.

slides.title: Dialogue Gives Stories Life
slides.storyContext: Arjun reads two versions of a story. First, 'Raja said something kind.' Second, 'Raja said, "You are the best friend ever!"' Maya notices: 'The first one is boring! But the second one is real. I feel like I am hearing Raja speak!' Dadi smiles: 'Inverted commas make stories feel alive. Readers hear the characters' real voices.'

slides.title: Apostrophes: Showing What Is Missing
slides.storyContext: Dadi teaches them a new mark. 'I am going becomes I'm. Do not becomes don't. See this tiny mark? It shows that letters are missing. We call it an apostrophe.'

points.label: What is an apostrophe?
points.text: A small curved mark (') that shows letters or sounds are missing in a shortened word.

points.label: Common contractions:
points.text: I'm (I am), don't (do not), can't (cannot), won't (will not), it's (it is), they're (they are).

example.problem: Write the short form: I will go to school
example.solution: I'll go to school.

slides.inSimpleWords: An apostrophe shows that some letters are left out of a word.

slides.title: Contractions in Everyday Speech
slides.storyContext: Maya and Arjun play a game with Dadi. She says full words, they say the short form. 'I am' becomes 'I'm.' 'Can not' becomes 'Can't.' 'It is' becomes 'It's.' They giggle at how much faster contractions sound when they speak. Dadi says: 'People often use contractions when speaking. Apostrophes help us write the way we talk.'

slides.title: Putting It All Together
slides.storyContext: At the end of the day, Dadi writes a sentence with all the marks: 'Maya asked, "Where are we going, Dadi?" "To the market," she said. "We will buy mangoes, bananas, and milk!"' The children clap. 'Now I see how the marks make the sentence sing!' says Maya.

example.problem: Rewrite this with correct punctuation: Arjun asked where did you go yesterday I went to school and then to the market with my mother and father
example.solution: Arjun asked, "Where did you go yesterday?" "I went to school and then to the market with my mother and father," she said.

slides.inSimpleWords: Punctuation marks work together to make sentences clear and beautiful.

image.alt: Putting It All Together — Punctuation

slides.title: Real Writing: A Letter to Dadi
slides.storyContext: Maya decides to write a letter to Dadi using all punctuation marks. She writes: 'Dear Dadi, Thank you for teaching us about punctuation! I now understand that full stops end sentences. Question marks let us ask. Commas separate ideas. Exclamation marks show excitement! Inverted commas help us hear people speak. Apostrophes shorten words. I can't believe one lesson changed my writing so much! Your granddaughter, Maya.' Dadi reads it and tears up. 'Perfect! Your writing is clear, alive, and beautiful!'

slides.title: Punctuation in Different Genres
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows them different types of writing: a story, a poem, a letter, and a newspaper article. 'Look how punctuation changes in each!' She points out that poems use dashes, stories use dialogue with inverted commas, letters use commas after greetings, and newspapers use exclamation marks for headlines. 'Punctuation is flexible. It adapts to what you are writing!'

slides.title: Challenge 1: Fix the Unpunctuated Sentence
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives them a mixed-up sentence with no punctuation. 'Your task: add all the punctuation marks you have learned so far.'

example.problem: I can't believe I won the race said Vikram running for joy
example.solution: "I can't believe I won the race!" said Vikram, running for joy.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now recognize where each punctuation mark belongs in a sentence.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Write Your Own Story Dialogue
slides.storyContext: Dadi challenges them: 'Write a short conversation between two characters. Use question marks, exclamation marks, inverted commas, commas in lists, and apostrophes. Show me you know them all!'

example.problem: Write a dialogue where one person asks a question with a list, and the other responds with excitement.
example.solution: "Do you like cricket, football, or tennis?" asked Priya. "I love all three!" exclaimed Arjun. "Let's play tomorrow!"

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now use all punctuation marks correctly in your own writing.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Punctuation Game
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives them one last task: 'Write a short sentence with a full stop, a question, a list with commas, and someone speaking in inverted commas. You are ready!'

example.problem: Write four sentences: 1) A statement about your school day. 2) A question about your favourite subject. 3) A list of three things you like. 4) Something someone said to you.
example.solution: 1) I had a good day at school today. 2) What is your favourite subject? 3) I like playing cricket, drawing, and reading stories. 4) My teacher said, "Always be curious."

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now use punctuation marks to write clear, beautiful sentences!

image.alt: Your Turn: The Punctuation Game — Punctuation

slides.title: What We Learned: Punctuation Magic

points.label: Full Stop (.)
points.text: Ends a complete sentence or statement.

points.label: Question Mark (?)
points.text: Ends a question—a sentence that asks something.

points.label: Comma (,)
points.text: Shows a small pause; separates items in a list or ideas.

points.label: Exclamation Mark (!)
points.text: Shows strong feelings like excitement, surprise, or fear.

points.label: Inverted Commas (" ")
points.text: Frame the exact words someone speaks.

points.label: Apostrophe (')
points.text: Shows letters are missing in a shortened word like I'm or don't.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Punctuation marks make our writing clear, just like traffic lights guide our cars!

slides.inSimpleWords: Punctuation marks are tools that help us write and read better.

image.alt: What We Learned: Punctuation Magic — Punctuation

subject: English
title: Ravi's Secret in the Library
hook: A shy boy discovers that reading stories teaches him to understand the world around him.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: a quiet fourth-grader learning to read deeper

characters.name: Mrs. Sharma
characters.role: the school librarian who guides him

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Ravi's classmate who loves asking questions

slides.title: Reading Comprehension
slides.storyContext: Ravi walks into the school library for the first time. Rows of books line the shelves like a maze. Mrs. Sharma smiles and says, 'Welcome! Let me teach you a secret: reading is not just about words—it is about understanding.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Reading comprehension means truly understanding what a story or passage tells us.

image.alt: Reading Comprehension — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: What Does Understanding Really Mean?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma explains: 'Many people can read words—fast and perfectly. But they might not understand the meaning. Reading comprehension is about asking yourself: What is happening? Why? What does it mean? How does it connect to me?' Ravi nods, beginning to understand the difference.

slides.title: Finding the Meaning
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma picks a small book about a farmer who finds a bird with a broken wing. 'Now, Ravi, I will read this story. Listen not just to the words, but to what the story teaches.' After reading, she asks questions: 'Who is the farmer helping? Why does he help? What does the farmer learn?' Ravi thinks hard and answers each one.
slides.inSimpleWords: When we read, we should ask ourselves: What is happening? Why? What does it mean?

image.alt: Finding the Meaning — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Reading Like a Detective
slides.storyContext: Priya joins Ravi and Mrs. Sharma. She says, 'I read stories like I am looking for clues in a mystery!' Mrs. Sharma nods approvingly. 'Exactly! Good readers look for clues in the words, in what characters do, and in how others react to them. These clues teach us the deeper meaning.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Reading carefully means looking for clues that help you understand the hidden meanings.

slides.title: The Big Picture: Why Comprehension Matters

points.label: What is reading comprehension?
points.text: It is understanding not just the words, but the ideas, feelings, and lessons in a passage.

points.label: Why does it matter?
points.text: Without comprehension, reading is just saying words. With it, reading teaches us about the world and ourselves.

slides.inSimpleWords: True reading means understanding the whole story, not just reading the words aloud.

slides.title: Finding the Main Idea
slides.storyContext: Priya joins them and picks a story about a girl who makes a rainwater tank for her village. 'This story has many sentences,' says Mrs. Sharma. 'But what is the big idea? What is the story really about?' Priya says, 'It is about helping people by being clever!' 'Yes!' laughs Mrs. Sharma.

points.label: What is the main idea?
points.text: The biggest, most important message or topic in a passage. It is not just one fact—it is what the whole story is about.

points.label: How to find it?
points.text: Ask yourself: If I had to tell someone the story in one sentence, what would I say? That is the main idea.

example.problem: Passage: Meena did not have clean water at home. She dug a well with her father. Now the whole village has water. What is the main idea?
example.solution: The main idea is: Meena and her father solved the village's water problem by digging a well.

slides.inSimpleWords: The main idea is the biggest message the passage is teaching us.

image.alt: Finding the Main Idea — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Main Idea Practice: Stories from Real Life
slides.storyContext: Ravi reads a story about a boy who learns to ride a bicycle. Mrs. Sharma asks, 'In one sentence, what is this story about?' Ravi thinks and says, 'It is about trying something hard until you succeed.' She smiles. 'Perfect! That is the main idea, the heart of the story.'

example.problem: Read this: Tina was shy. At the school talent show, she sang a song. Her voice was beautiful. Everyone clapped. She felt proud. What is the main idea?
example.solution: The main idea is: Tina overcame her shyness and discovered she had a beautiful voice that others admired.

slides.inSimpleWords: The main idea connects all the details into one big lesson or message.

slides.title: Main Idea vs. Details
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma teaches the difference. She reads: 'Rohan was a good student. He studied hard. He came to school on time. He helped his classmates. His teachers loved him.' She asks: 'What are the details?' Priya lists them. 'Now, what is the main idea that ties all these details together?' Ravi answers: 'Rohan is a responsible and kind person!' 'Exactly!' says Mrs. Sharma.

slides.title: Finding Supporting Details
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma reads a story about a boy named Akshay who saves money to buy his mother a gift. She asks, 'What details tell us that Akshay is kind? What details show he is saving hard?' Ravi finds these: 'He does chores. He does not buy sweets. He counts his money.' 'Exactly!' says Mrs. Sharma. 'Details are the small facts that prove the main idea.'

points.label: What are supporting details?
points.text: Small facts, descriptions, or examples in a passage that explain or prove the main idea.

points.label: Why do we find them?
points.text: They help us understand and believe the main idea. They give us proof.

example.problem: Main idea: Deepa is a fast runner. Find two supporting details from this passage: 'Deepa ran in the school race yesterday. She finished before all the other children. Everyone cheered for her.'
example.solution: Detail 1: Deepa ran in the school race and finished before all the other children. Detail 2: Everyone cheered for her.

slides.inSimpleWords: Supporting details are like bricks that build up the main idea.

image.alt: Finding Supporting Details — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Spotting Details: Proof for Ideas
slides.storyContext: Priya reads about a girl named Isha who shares her lunch. Mrs. Sharma asks, 'What details show Isha is generous?' Priya finds: 'She gave away her food. She did it without being asked. She smiled while giving.' These small details prove the main idea: Isha is kind and generous.

example.problem: Main idea: The library is a magical place. Find three supporting details.
example.solution: Details could be: (1) Books line the shelves like treasure. (2) Quiet corners invite you to dream. (3) Every story opens a new world.

slides.inSimpleWords: Details are the specific facts that show the main idea is true.

slides.title: How Details Build Confidence
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices that when Mrs. Sharma reads him a passage, he can now find details that prove the main idea. He thinks: 'I am like a detective collecting evidence. Each detail is a clue that confirms my understanding.' This feeling of understanding makes him confident and excited to read more.

slides.title: Understanding Characters: Their Feelings and Choices
slides.storyContext: A story tells of a girl named Isha who shares her lunch with a hungry child even though she is hungry too. 'Why did Isha do this?' asks Mrs. Sharma. Ravi answers, 'Because she is kind and cares.' 'Yes,' says Mrs. Sharma. 'When we read, we understand not just what people do, but why they do it and how they feel.'

points.label: What should we understand about characters?
points.text: Their feelings, their choices, why they act that way, and what they learn.

points.label: How do we know?
points.text: From what they do, what they say, and how other characters react to them.

example.problem: Arjun finds a stray dog on the street. He takes it home, feeds it, and gives it a bed. What does this tell us about Arjun?
example.solution: This tells us that Arjun is kind, caring, and brave. He does not fear helping someone in need. He is compassionate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding characters means knowing what they feel and why they make their choices.

image.alt: Understanding Characters: Their Feelings and Choices — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Character Analysis: What Choices Reveal
slides.storyContext: Ravi reads a story about a boy who gives away his lunch to help a friend, even though he is hungry. Mrs. Sharma asks, 'What does this choice tell us about the boy's character?' Ravi thinks carefully: 'He puts his friend's needs before his own. He is loyal and selfless.'

example.problem: Neha studies hard even when her friends want to play. What does this show about her character?
example.solution: This shows that Neha is disciplined, focused on her goals, and willing to make sacrifices for her future. She values education.

slides.inSimpleWords: What a character chooses to do reveals who they are inside.

slides.title: Understanding Why Characters Act
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a story where a character does something mean. She asks Mrs. Sharma: 'Does that mean the character is bad?' Mrs. Sharma replies: 'Not necessarily. Good readers understand that characters have reasons for their actions—fear, sadness, or misunderstanding. When we understand their feelings, we understand their choices.' This teaches Ravi that real understanding is deeper than judging.

slides.title: Connecting the Passage to Real Life
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma reads a story about a boy who must walk far to bring water. Ravi says suddenly, 'My grandmother told me the same thing! In her village, they had no taps.' Mrs. Sharma nods happily: 'Yes! When we connect stories to our own lives, we understand them better and they become real to us.'

points.label: Why connect to real life?
points.text: It helps us care about the story and understand it deeply. We see that the story's lesson applies to us too.

points.label: How do we do it?
points.text: Ask: Have I seen this situation? Do I know someone like this character? How would I feel? What would I do?

example.problem: A story is about a girl who is nervous before her first day at a new school. How can you connect this to your life?
example.solution: I can connect it by remembering my first day at school. I was nervous too. I understand how the girl feels. The story teaches me that new things can be scary but also exciting.

slides.inSimpleWords: Connecting stories to our lives makes them meaningful and helps us learn.

image.alt: Connecting the Passage to Real Life — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: My Story, Their Story: Making Connections
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a story about a girl who is scared of the dark. She tells Mrs. Sharma, 'I used to be scared too! But the girl learns that the dark is not scary once you understand it.' Mrs. Sharma smiles. 'Now the story has become part of your life, and it teaches you something real.'

example.problem: A story is about a farmer who does not give up when his crops fail. How can you connect this to your life?
example.solution: I can connect it by thinking of a time when I failed a test. The farmer's persistence teaches me that one failure is not the end. I should try again.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you connect a story to your own experiences, it becomes real and meaningful.

slides.title: Asking Questions While Reading
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a story and stops. 'I have questions!' she says. 'Why did the boy leave his village? Where is he going? Will he come back?' Mrs. Sharma smiles: 'Perfect! Good readers ask questions. It keeps your mind active like a detective searching for clues.'

points.label: What kinds of questions help?
points.text: Why did this happen? How did the character feel? What will happen next? What does this mean? What is the lesson?

points.label: When should we ask?
points.text: Before reading, during reading, and after reading. Questions keep us thinking and understanding.

example.problem: You read: 'The farmer looked at the dark clouds and put his tools away.' What questions can you ask?
example.solution: Why did the farmer put his tools away? Is he worried about rain? What will he do now? Is he concerned about his crops?

slides.inSimpleWords: Asking questions while reading helps us think deeply and understand better.

image.alt: Asking Questions While Reading — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: The Power of Curious Questions
slides.storyContext: Ravi reads about a character who makes an unexpected choice. He asks, 'Why did she do that? What was she thinking? Will she regret it?' Mrs. Sharma praises him. 'Your questions show you are truly engaged with the story. You are not just reading words—you are thinking like the character.'

example.problem: You read: 'Aman gave away his favorite toy to a new friend.' Ask three good questions about this.
example.solution: (1) Why did Aman give away his favorite toy? (2) How did the new friend feel? (3) What does this tell us about Aman's character?

slides.inSimpleWords: Good questions help you understand why characters do what they do.

slides.title: Reading a Whole Passage: A Real Test
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma gives Ravi a full story about two best friends: 'Asha and Preet were inseparable. One day, Preet found a beautiful stone on the beach. Asha asked if she could have it, but Preet said no. Days passed and they did not speak. Then Asha understood—the stone was not important. Preet's friendship was. Asha apologized. Preet smiled and gave her the stone.' After reading, Ravi answers everything correctly, showing true understanding.

slides.title: Reading a Whole Passage Carefully
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma gives Ravi a full story to read: 'The Wise Old Teacher.' After Ravi reads, he answers these questions: Main idea? Supporting details? What does the teacher teach? How do the students feel? What is the lesson for us? By the end, Ravi realizes he understood everything—and it made him happy.

example.problem: Read this passage: 'Maya was afraid to try swimming. She stayed on the shore. One day, her friend jumped in happily. Maya watched and saw it was safe. She took a breath and jumped too. Now she swims every day and loves it.' Answer: (1) Main idea? (2) Why was Maya afraid? (3) What changed her mind? (4) What does this teach us?
example.solution: (1) Main idea: Maya overcame her fear of swimming by watching her friend and being brave. (2) Maya was afraid because she did not know how to swim and thought it might not be safe. (3) She saw her friend enjoying it and felt safer. (4) The passage teaches us that we can overcome fear by trying new things, watching others, and being brave.

slides.inSimpleWords: When we read carefully and ask questions, even long stories become clear.

image.alt: Reading a Whole Passage Carefully — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Challenge 1: Find the Main Idea and Details
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma gives Ravi a new passage and asks him to identify the main idea and find three supporting details without her help.

example.problem: Read and answer: 'Rishi loved science. He built a model of the solar system. He read books about planets. He even watched videos about space travel. His teacher praised his work.' Find the main idea and three supporting details.
example.solution: Main idea: Rishi is passionate about science and learns deeply. Details: (1) He built a solar system model. (2) He read books about planets. (3) He watched space travel videos.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now identify main ideas and find the details that support them.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Analyze a Character's Choices
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Read a story about a character and explain: What choice does the character make? Why do they make it? What does it reveal about their character? What would you do?'

example.problem: A boy finds money in the park. He does not keep it but looks for the owner. Why might he do this? What does this reveal about him?
example.solution: He might be honest and kind. He knows that the money belongs to someone who needs it. This reveals he is moral and thinks of others. I would do the same because honesty is important.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now understand why characters make their choices and what it shows.

slides.title: Your Turn: Be a Reading Detective
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma hands Ravi a new story. 'Now you are the teacher. Read this and find: the main idea, the biggest feeling in the story, a character's choice and why they made it, and what the story teaches us. You are ready!'

example.problem: Read this story: 'Rohan had only one rupee. He could buy candy or a notebook for his school. He wanted candy but bought the notebook because his pencil was broken. At school, he wrote a beautiful essay and his teacher praised him. Rohan felt proud.' Now answer: What is the main idea? Why did Rohan choose the notebook? What does he learn? What does this teach us?
example.solution: Main idea: Rohan makes a wise choice by buying what he needs instead of what he wants. Why: His pencil was broken and he needed a notebook for school. What he learns: Choosing wisely brings more happiness than choosing candy. What it teaches us: Thinking ahead and choosing what we need instead of what we want is mature and leads to pride and success.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now read any story, ask good questions, and truly understand it!

image.alt: Your Turn: Be a Reading Detective — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Ravi's Journey: From Shy to Smart Reader
slides.storyContext: By the end of their lessons, Ravi transforms. He was once afraid to speak up in class. Now he raises his hand confidently to share his thoughts about stories. 'I understand!' he says proudly. Mrs. Sharma beams: 'You have become a true reader. You do not just read words—you think deeply about what they mean.'

slides.title: Reading Changes Everything
slides.storyContext: Ravi realizes that reading comprehension is not just a skill for school. It helps him understand his friends better. When Priya is sad, he reads her face and offers to help. When his grandmother tells stories, he listens for the deeper meaning. Reading has made him wiser about people and the world around him.

slides.title: What We Learned: Becoming a Smart Reader

points.label: Main Idea
points.text: The biggest message the passage teaches. It is like the heart of the story.

points.label: Supporting Details
points.text: Small facts that prove or explain the main idea. They are like bricks in a wall.

points.label: Characters
points.text: Understand their feelings, choices, and what they learn. Ask why they do what they do.

points.label: Connection
points.text: Link the story to your own life to make it real and meaningful.

points.label: Ask Questions
points.text: Before, during, and after reading. Questions keep your mind thinking like a detective.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Smart reading is not just reading words—it is understanding the whole story and what it means.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading comprehension means understanding the story deeply, not just reading the words.

image.alt: What We Learned: Becoming a Smart Reader — Reading Comprehension

subject: English
title: The Rhyme School: Where Words Dance
hook: When words rhyme, they make music; when they repeat, they make magic.

characters.name: Zara
characters.role: a girl who loves the music of words

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: Zara's friend who discovers rhythm

characters.name: Poet Uncle
characters.role: a friendly poet who teaches them at the community center

slides.title: Poetry and Rhymes
slides.storyContext: Zara and Vikram arrive at the community center for Poet Uncle's class. The room smells of paper and chai. On the wall are colorful poems with words that dance and rhyme. 'Welcome,' says Poet Uncle, 'to the place where words become music.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is when words make beautiful sounds and carry special feelings.

image.alt: Poetry and Rhymes — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Why Do People Write Poetry?
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle asks them: 'Why do you think people write poems instead of just stories?' Zara thinks and says, 'Maybe because poems are more beautiful?' Vikram adds, 'And they rhyme, so they stick in our brains!' Poet Uncle nods: 'Exactly! Poems let us express feelings in a special way—through sound, rhythm, and beauty. Poems make words dance.'

slides.title: Words with a Beat
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle begins by clapping. 'Listen! This is rhythm. Now listen to these words: cat, bat, sat, mat. Do you hear how they sound alike? That is rhyme.' He claps faster and the words dance to the beat. Zara and Vikram laugh and clap too, saying the rhyming words together like a song.
slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyming words sound like music because their endings sound the same.

image.alt: Words with a Beat — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Poetry Is Everywhere Around Us
slides.storyContext: Zara says, 'I hear rhymes in songs my mother sings!' Vikram adds, 'And in the nursery rhymes from when I was small!' Poet Uncle nods wisely. 'Exactly! Poetry is not just in books. It is in lullabies, in folk songs, in street chants, in Bollywood movies. Poetry surrounds us. We just have to listen.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is everywhere—in songs, in chants, in the words we hear every day.

slides.title: What Poetry Really Is

points.label: What makes something poetry?
points.text: Poetry uses special language and sounds to express feelings and ideas in a beautiful and memorable way.

points.label: Key features:
points.text: Rhyming words, rhythm or beat, repetition, vivid images, and strong emotions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is writing that uses beauty and music to touch our hearts.

slides.title: What Are Rhyming Words?
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle writes on the board: 'rain, pain, train, chain, main.' 'See? They all end with 'ain' sound. When words end with the same sound, they rhyme. Rhyming words are like friends holding hands—they belong together.' Vikram shouts excitedly, 'I see it! Like moon and soon, or day and play!'

points.label: What is rhyme?
points.text: When two or more words have the same ending sound, they rhyme. Like 'cat' and 'bat'—both end with the 'at' sound.

points.label: Examples of rhyming pairs:
points.text: night and light, tree and bee, smile and mile, king and sing, door and more.

example.problem: Which word rhymes with 'house'? mouse, table, or food?
example.solution: mouse rhymes with 'house' because they both end with the 'ous' sound.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyming words sound like a pair—they have the same ending sound.

image.alt: What Are Rhyming Words? — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Rhyme Hunt: Finding Rhyming Pairs
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle asks Zara and Vikram to find rhyming pairs in a list of words. Zara finds: 'sky and high!' Vikram finds: 'song and long!' They cheer as Poet Uncle writes more rhyming pairs on the board. 'Now you hear the music! Rhyming words sing together.'

example.problem: Find three rhyming pairs from this list: sea, free, jump, bee, hump, tea
example.solution: Pair 1: sea and free (both end with 'ee'). Pair 2: sea and tea (both end with 'ea'). Pair 3: jump and hump (both end with 'ump').

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you hear the sound pattern, finding rhyming pairs becomes easy and fun.

slides.title: How Rhymes Stick in Our Brains
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle teaches them an old nursery rhyme and asks them to repeat it three times. Soon, they can recite it without looking! 'See?' he says. 'Rhyming words are sticky. They lodge in our memory because the sound patterns make them unforgettable. That is why songs use rhymes—so we remember them!'

slides.title: The Music of Rhythm in Poetry
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads a poem aloud with strong rhythm: 'Clap-clap, the rain falls, plip-plop, the rain calls.' He stamps his foot to show the beat. 'Every poem has a rhythm—a heartbeat. When we read it right, the poem dances!' Zara closes her eyes and hears the song inside the words.

points.label: What is rhythm?
points.text: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that make a poem sound like music or a heartbeat.

points.label: Why does it matter?
points.text: Rhythm makes a poem fun to say aloud. It sticks in our memory. It makes the message stronger and more beautiful.

example.problem: Read aloud with rhythm: 'In the morning, light breaks, in the night, darkness wakes.' Where is the beat strong?
example.solution: The beat is strong on: MORning, LIGHT breaks, NIGHT, DARKness wakes. The rhythm sounds like: boom-boom, boom-boom.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhythm is the heartbeat of a poem—it makes words dance and sing.

image.alt: The Music of Rhythm in Poetry — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Feeling the Rhythm: Clapping Along
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle teaches a poem with a strong rhythm: 'The sun shines bright, the day is long, the birds all sing a happy song.' Zara and Vikram clap along: CLAP-clap CLAP-clap. 'Yes!' cheers Poet Uncle. 'When you feel the rhythm, the poem comes alive. Your body knows the beat before your mind does!'

example.problem: Mark the strong beat in: 'The cat sat on the MAT, the dog had a HAT.'
example.solution: The CAT sat on the MAT, the DOG had a HAT. The strong beat is on: CAT, MAT, DOG, HAT.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you hear the rhythm, you can clap, dance, or march to the poem's beat.

slides.title: The Magic of Sound: Why Poems Sound Better Aloud
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads a poem silently, then aloud. 'Notice the difference?' he asks. When read silently, Zara thinks it is nice. But when read aloud, with rhythm and flow, it comes alive! Vikram notices: 'It is like the words wake up! They have power when we say them out loud!' Poet Uncle smiles: 'Poetry is meant to be heard, not just read.'

slides.title: Repetition: When Words Come Back
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads a short poem: 'The sun, the sun, the golden sun, brings joy to everyone. The sun, the sun, the golden sun, shines till the day is done.' Vikram notices, 'The sun, the sun comes back three times!' Poet Uncle nods, 'Yes! That is repetition. A word or phrase comes back again and again, like an echo. It makes the poem more beautiful and helps us remember.'

points.label: What is repetition?
points.text: When the same word or phrase appears many times in a poem. Like an echo that comes back.

points.label: Why do poets use it?
points.text: To make certain ideas stand out, to create rhythm, to make the poem easy to remember, and to show that something is very important.

example.problem: Add repetition to this line: 'The wind blows through the trees.' Make it more powerful.
example.solution: The wind, the wind, the wind blows strong, through the trees all day long.

slides.inSimpleWords: Repetition is when a word or phrase comes back, making the poem more powerful.

image.alt: Repetition: When Words Come Back — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Repetition Creates Power and Memory
slides.storyContext: Zara reads: 'Hope, hope, hope shines bright, hope lights up the dark night!' Poet Uncle explains, 'By repeating 'hope,' the poet makes us feel it strongly. We remember it. Our hearts beat with hope.' Vikram adds, 'It is like how 'Diwali, Diwali' feels more exciting than just 'Diwali' once!'

example.problem: Use repetition to make this line stronger: 'The river flows.'
example.solution: The river flows, flows, flows to the sea, wild and free and free and free.

slides.inSimpleWords: Repeating words makes them stick in our minds and feel more important.

slides.title: Simple Rhyme Schemes: AA BB CC
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle teaches how to map rhymes. 'Look at this poem: The cat sat on a mat (A), and looked quite fat (A). The dog ran in the bog (B), and danced like a frog (B). The letters show us which lines rhyme!' Zara draws the pattern and laughs, 'It is like a puzzle!'

points.label: What is a rhyme scheme?
points.text: A pattern that shows which lines of a poem rhyme. We use letters: A, B, C and so on.

points.label: Common patterns for children:
points.text: AA BB (couplets): two lines rhyme, then two more rhyme. AB AB: first and third rhyme, second and fourth rhyme.

example.problem: Mark the rhyme scheme: 'The little bird flew high (A), into the blue sky (A). It sang a sweet song (B), the whole day long (B).'
example.solution: Line 1 (high) = A, Line 2 (sky) = A, Line 3 (song) = B, Line 4 (long) = B. Rhyme scheme: AA BB.

slides.inSimpleWords: A rhyme scheme is a map that shows which lines in a poem rhyme.

image.alt: Simple Rhyme Schemes: AA BB CC — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Mapping Rhyme Schemes: A, B, C Pattern
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shows Zara a more complex poem: 'The cat is red (A), sleeping in bed (A), dreaming of mice (B), oh, how very nice (B), running through wheat (C), can't wait to eat (C).' Zara carefully maps it: AA BB CC. 'Now I see the pattern!' she cries. 'The poem builds like building blocks!'

example.problem: Mark the rhyme scheme: 'I love to play (A), every single day (A), in the park so green (B), the prettiest place I've seen (B), with friends so true (C), and skies of blue (C).'
example.solution: AA BB CC. Each pair of lines rhymes together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Learning rhyme schemes helps you see how a poet builds a poem's structure.

slides.title: Different Rhyme Schemes, Different Feelings
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle explains: 'A poem with AA BB feels like it is moving in pairs, like a march. But a poem with ABAB feels like it is weaving back and forth, like a dance.' He reads examples and asks them to feel the difference. Vikram notices: 'Each rhyme scheme has its own music!'

slides.title: Rhyme in Our Lives: Nursery Rhymes and Songs
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle asks, 'Who knows a nursery rhyme?' Both children giggle and sing: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are.' Poet Uncle claps: 'Yes! These are poems. They have rhyme, rhythm, and repetition. Songs are poems too! Even in Bollywood, rhyming words make songs stick in our heads.'

points.label: Where do we find rhyming poetry?
points.text: Nursery rhymes, lullabies, songs, Bollywood movie songs, greeting cards, funny verses, and stories in verse.

points.label: Why is rhyming poetry popular?
points.text: It is easy to remember, fun to sing, and the rhythm and rhyme make it beautiful.

example.problem: Make a simple rhyming couplet about your school day.
example.solution: I went to school to learn and play, and had a wonderful, happy day!

slides.inSimpleWords: Nursery rhymes and songs are poems that rhyme—they are fun and easy to remember.

image.alt: Rhyme in Our Lives: Nursery Rhymes and Songs — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Bollywood Poetry: Songs That Stick
slides.storyContext: Vikram suddenly starts singing a Bollywood song he knows. Poet Uncle smiles. 'Exactly! That song has rhyming words that make it unforgettable. 'Kuch kuch hota hai' rhymes with 'tere dil mein.' The rhythm and rhyme make it dance in our hearts and brains forever.'

example.problem: Think of a song you know. What words rhyme? Can you hear the rhythm?
example.solution: In many Hindi songs, words like 'pyar' and 'dil,' 'raat' and 'baat' rhyme. When sung, the rhythm makes them stick in our memory.

slides.inSimpleWords: Songs in movies and folk music use rhyme and rhythm to stay in our hearts.

slides.title: Creating a Simple Rhyming Poem
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle asks them to write a four-line poem about monsoon. Zara and Vikram work together: 'The rain goes pitter-patter, (A) falling on the ground, (B) the sky and clouds do chatter, (A) with such a gentle sound. (B)' Poet Uncle reads it aloud with rhythm and smile. 'Perfect! You are poets now!'

example.problem: Write a four-line rhyming poem about your favorite season using the AA BB pattern.
example.solution: Example: Summer is hot and bright, (A) the sun shines every day, (A) we swim and play all night, (B) and run outside to play. (B)

slides.inSimpleWords: Anyone can write a rhyming poem if they follow the rhythm and find rhyming words.

image.alt: Creating a Simple Rhyming Poem — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: The Poet Inside You
slides.storyContext: After writing their first poem, Zara and Vikram feel different. Zara whispers: 'I never thought I could be a poet!' Poet Uncle puts a hand on each shoulder: 'Everyone has a poet inside. Poetry is just using words in a beautiful way to express what your heart feels. You have already started.'

slides.title: Challenge 1: Find Rhyming Pairs in Poems
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives them a poem and asks them to find all the rhyming pairs without help. This time they are truly ready.

example.problem: Find the rhyming pairs: 'The moon shines bright, guiding the night, while stars dance high, in the dark sky, trees sway slow, as cool winds blow.'
example.solution: Pair 1: bright and night. Pair 2: high and sky. Pair 3: slow and blow.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now identify rhyming pairs and understand the music of a poem.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Write a Poem with Repetition
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle challenges them: 'Write a four-line poem using repetition. Repeat a word or phrase to make your idea powerful and memorable.'

example.problem: Write a poem where one word or phrase is repeated at least twice to create power.
example.solution: Example: Love, love, love fills my heart, love is where we start, love brings us near, love makes all clear.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now use repetition to make your poems more powerful and memorable.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Map a Rhyme Scheme
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives them a poem and asks: 'Identify the rhyme scheme using letters A, B, C and so on.'

example.problem: Map the rhyme scheme: 'The apple is red (A), from the tree where I spread (A), the seeds in the soil (B), from years of hard toil (B).'
example.solution: The rhyme scheme is AA BB.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now map out the rhyme patterns in any poem.

slides.title: Your Turn: Become a Poet
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives them a challenge: 'Write a six-line poem about something you love. Use rhyming words, add a rhythm when you read it aloud, and try using repetition at least once. Make it your own.'

example.problem: Write a six-line rhyming poem (AA BB CC pattern) about cricket or a festival or an animal, with at least one repeated word or phrase.
example.solution: Example about cricket: The cricket bat swings left and right, (A) hitting the ball with all its might. (A) The ball flies high into the air, (B) the fielders run and jump with care. (B) Cricket, cricket, such joy and fun, (C) we play until the day is done. (C)

slides.inSimpleWords: You can now create your own poems by using rhyme, rhythm, and repetition!

image.alt: Your Turn: Become a Poet — Poetry and Rhymes

slides.title: Poets Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: By the end of class, Zara realizes something magical: 'Poet Uncle, are we poets now?' He smiles wisely: 'Yes. But so are the people who write film songs, the mothers who sing lullabies, the street musicians, the people who write greeting cards. Poetry is not just for books. It is in the heart of anyone who loves beautiful words.'

slides.title: What We Learned: The Magic of Poetry

points.label: Rhyming Words
points.text: Words that end with the same sound. Like 'cat' and 'bat.' They make poetry musical.

points.label: Rhythm
points.text: The heartbeat of a poem. It is the pattern of strong and soft beats that makes words dance.

points.label: Repetition
points.text: When the same word or phrase comes back again and again. It makes ideas strong and helps us remember.

points.label: Rhyme Scheme
points.text: A map showing which lines rhyme, using letters like AA BB or AB AB.

points.label: Poetry All Around
points.text: We find rhyming poems in nursery rhymes, songs, and even Bollywood movies. Poetry is everywhere!

points.label: Remember
points.text: When you write or read a poem, listen to the music in the words. That is the soul of poetry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is the beautiful music of words—rhymes, rhythm, and feeling all together.

image.alt: What We Learned: The Magic of Poetry — Poetry and Rhymes

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Market Day Adventure
hook: Help Priya buy supplies for the school fair — measure lengths, count money, and tell time!

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: curious student planning a fair

characters.name: Uncle Raj
characters.role: vendor at the local market

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: Priya's best friend helping with math

slides.title: Time, Money, Measurement
slides.storyContext: Priya's school is having a fair tomorrow. She needs to go shopping at the market, buy things with rupees, measure fabric, and make sure she's back in time!

image.alt: Time, Money, Measurement — Time, Money, Measurement

slides.title: The Fair Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya and Rohan have ₹500 to spend. They need to buy: colored paper (₹120), fabric for a booth (₹180), and snacks for helpers (₹150). But they must also measure how much fabric fits the booth and get home before 5:00 PM. It is now 2:15 PM.
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya has a budget and a time limit to finish shopping and get home.

image.alt: The Fair Challenge — Time, Money, Measurement

slides.title: Telling Time in Hours and Minutes
slides.storyContext: At the market, Priya looks at Uncle Raj's big clock. The hour hand points between 2 and 3, and the minute hand points to 3. What time is it?

points.label: Hour hand (short)
points.text: moves slowly, shows the hour

points.label: Minute hand (long)
points.text: moves faster, shows minutes past the hour

points.label: Clock face
points.text: has 12 numbers; minute hand at 3 means 15 minutes past the hour

example.problem: If hour hand is between 2 and 3, and minute hand is at 3, what time is it?
example.solution: 2:15 (2 hours and 15 minutes, or quarter past 2)

slides.inSimpleWords: The short hand tells hours, the long hand tells minutes. Together they show the exact time.

image.alt: Telling Time in Hours and Minutes — Time, Money, Measurement

slides.title: Reading Different Clock Times
slides.storyContext: Priya practices with Uncle Raj. He points to different positions on his big clock.

points.label: Minute hand at 6
points.text: = 30 minutes (half past)

points.label: Minute hand at 9
points.text: = 45 minutes (quarter to the next hour)

points.label: Minute hand at 12
points.text: = 0 minutes (o'clock / on the hour)

example.problem: If hour hand is at 3 and minute hand is at 6, what time is it?
example.solution: 3:30 (half past 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice reading the clock by looking at where both hands point.

slides.title: Rohan's Time Trick
slides.storyContext: Rohan teaches Priya a trick: 'Remember, the minute hand moves 5 minutes for every number on the clock. So if it's at 3, that's 3 × 5 = 15 minutes. If it's at 6, that's 6 × 5 = 30 minutes—half past!' Priya practices reading different times.
slides.inSimpleWords: The minute hand is tricky. Use the rule: each number equals 5 minutes.

slides.title: Time in Minutes: How Long Until 5:00 PM?
slides.storyContext: Priya starts shopping at 2:15 PM and wants to leave by 5:00 PM. How many minutes does she have?

points.label: From 2:15 to 5:00
points.text: is 2 hours and 45 minutes

points.label: In minutes only
points.text: 2 hours = 120 minutes; add 45 minutes = 165 minutes total

points.label: Quick counting
points.text: Count by 5s on clock face to find minutes: 15, 20, 25... up to 60 for a full hour

example.problem: Priya starts at 2:15 PM. She has until 5:00 PM. How many minutes?
example.solution: From 2:15 to 3:15 = 60 min, 3:15 to 4:15 = 60 min, 4:15 to 5:00 = 45 min. Total = 165 minutes

slides.inSimpleWords: Count how many hours and minutes have passed to find the time difference.

image.alt: Time in Minutes: How Long Until 5:00 PM? — Time, Money, Measurement

slides.title: Quarter Past, Half Past, Quarter To
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj calls out times as Priya browses. '2:15 is quarter past 2!' '2:30 is half past 2—the minute hand points straight down!' '2:45 is quarter to 3—almost there!' Priya writes these down so she remembers.
slides.inSimpleWords: Special names for common times: quarter past (15 min), half past (30 min), quarter to (45 min).

slides.title: Special Time Words
slides.storyContext: These special names appear on clocks and in daily life all the time.

points.label: Quarter past
points.text: 15 minutes after the hour (e.g., quarter past 2 = 2:15)

points.label: Half past
points.text: 30 minutes after the hour (e.g., half past 2 = 2:30)

points.label: Quarter to
points.text: 45 minutes after, or 15 minutes before next hour (e.g., quarter to 3 = 2:45)

example.problem: What time is quarter past 4? Half past 7? Quarter to 6?
example.solution: Quarter past 4 = 4:15. Half past 7 = 7:30. Quarter to 6 = 5:45.

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize these three special times to read clocks faster and understand spoken time better.

slides.title: Indian Rupees: Counting Money
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj shows Priya coins: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 coins and ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100 notes. Priya has 5 notes of ₹100. How much money does she have?

points.label: Coins
points.text: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 (small metal money)

points.label: Adding money
points.text: Count all coins and notes together to find total rupees

example.problem: Priya has 5 notes of ₹100 each. How much rupees total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Count your rupees and notes to know how much money you have to spend.

image.alt: Indian Rupees: Counting Money — Time, Money, Measurement

slides.title: Counting Coins and Notes Together
slides.storyContext: Priya counts her money: 2 × ₹100 notes, 3 × ₹50 notes, 2 × ₹20 notes, 5 × ₹1 coins. How much total?
slides.inSimpleWords: When you have many types of coins and notes, add each group first, then add all groups together.

slides.title: Making Change at the Market
slides.storyContext: Priya buys colored paper for ₹120. She gives Uncle Raj a ₹100 note and a ₹50 note (₹150 total). 'How much change?' asks Priya. Uncle Raj counts: '₹150 minus ₹120 = ₹30 change.' He hands her three ₹10 notes.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you pay more than the price, the extra money you get back is called change.

slides.title: Finding Change from a Purchase
slides.storyContext: Change = what you paid − what you owed. Always subtract the price from the money you gave.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Change = Money given − Price

points.label: Example
points.text: You give ₹100, item costs ₹75, change = ₹100 − ₹75 = ₹25

points.label: Check your change
points.text: Always count and verify the coins or notes you receive

example.problem: Priya pays ₹150 for colored paper worth ₹120. How much change?
example.solution: ₹150 − ₹120 = ₹30 change. She could get 3 × ₹10 or 1 × ₹20 + 1 × ₹10, etc.

slides.inSimpleWords: Change is the money left over. Subtract the price from what you gave.

slides.title: Adding Expenses: Does Priya Have Enough?
slides.storyContext: Priya's shopping list: colored paper ₹120, fabric ₹180, snacks ₹150. Does she stay within ₹500?

points.label: Check budget
points.text: Total cost ₹450 is less than ₹500, so she has enough

points.label: Money left
points.text: ₹500 − ₹450 = ₹50 remaining

example.problem: Priya spends ₹120, ₹180, and ₹150. Does she stay under ₹500?

slides.inSimpleWords: Add up all your costs to check if you have enough money and change left over.

slides.title: Special Deals at the Market
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj shows Priya a deal: 'Buy 2 metres of fabric for ₹180, or buy 1 metre for ₹100. Two metres is better value!' Priya realizes: 2 metres for ₹180 = ₹90 per metre, vs 1 metre for ₹100. She takes the 2-metre deal.
slides.inSimpleWords: Compare prices to find the best deal. Sometimes bigger amounts cost less per item.

slides.title: Measuring Length in Metres and Centimetres
slides.storyContext: The booth needs 4 metres of fabric. Uncle Raj's tape measure shows metres (m) and centimetres (cm). How many centimetres is 4 metres?

points.label: 1 metre
points.text: = 100 centimetres (cm)

points.label: Measuring tape
points.text: shows both metres and centimetres

points.label: Converting
points.text: multiply metres × 100 to get centimetres

example.problem: The booth needs 4 metres of fabric. How many centimetres?
example.solution: 4 metres × 100 = 400 centimetres

slides.inSimpleWords: Bigger things are measured in metres, smaller in centimetres. 100 cm = 1 metre.

slides.title: Converting Metres to Centimetres
slides.storyContext: Priya needs to convert different fabric lengths.

points.label: 2 metres
points.text: = 2 × 100 = 200 centimetres

points.label: 5 metres
points.text: = 5 × 100 = 500 centimetres

points.label: 10 metres
points.text: = 10 × 100 = 1000 centimetres

example.problem: Convert 3 metres, 6 metres, and 8 metres to centimetres.

slides.inSimpleWords: To convert metres to centimetres, always multiply by 100.

slides.title: Measuring the Booth
slides.storyContext: Priya holds one end of Uncle Raj's tape measure. 'Stretch it along the booth,' he says. Priya counts: 1 metre, 2 metres, 3 metres, 4 metres. 'Perfect!' says Uncle Raj. 'Four metres of fabric is enough. That's 400 centimetres of colour!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use a measuring tape to find real lengths of things around you.

slides.title: Estimating vs. Measuring
slides.storyContext: Rohan guesses the booth is '3 metres long.' Priya measures with the tape: 4 metres. 'My guess was wrong!' says Rohan. 'Estimation is close but not exact. Only measuring with a tool is exact.'

points.label: Estimating
points.text: guessing a measurement without tools (rough idea)

points.label: Measuring
points.text: using a ruler or tape to get the exact length

points.label: When to estimate
points.text: when you need a quick rough idea; when to measure, when you need exact answers

example.problem: Rohan guesses 3m, the tape shows 4m. What's the error?
example.solution: Rohan's estimate was 1m too short (error of 25%).

slides.inSimpleWords: Estimating is a quick guess; measuring is exact. Always measure for important jobs.

slides.title: Smaller Measurements: Millimetres
slides.storyContext: Priya notices detailed trim in the booth. 'How small is this edge?' she asks. Uncle Raj shows her: 'This is 50 millimetres. There are 10 millimetres in 1 centimetre, and 100 centimetres in 1 metre. So 1 metre = 1000 millimetres!'
slides.inSimpleWords: For very small things, use millimetres (mm). 10 mm = 1 cm.

slides.title: The Full Length Scale: mm to Metre
slides.storyContext: Understanding all the units helps Priya measure anything, from tiny details to large booth dimensions.

points.label: Millimetre (mm)
points.text: smallest unit, for very tiny things (width of a thread)

points.label: Centimetre (cm)
points.text: 10 mm = 1 cm, for small objects (width of a pencil)

points.label: Metre (m)
points.text: 100 cm = 1 m = 1000 mm, for large items (booth, room)

example.problem: Express 450 cm in metres and centimetres. Also in millimetres.
example.solution: 450 cm = 4 metres and 50 cm. Also = 4500 mm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the right unit for the right job: mm for tiny, cm for small, m for large.

slides.title: Full Shopping Math: Priya's Complete Day
slides.storyContext: Let's put it all together. Priya starts at 2:15 PM with ₹500. She buys: colored paper ₹120, fabric (4 m = 400 cm) ₹180, snacks ₹150. She must leave by 5:00 PM.

points.label: Time to shop
points.text: 2:15 PM to 5:00 PM = 2 hours 45 minutes = 165 minutes

points.label: Fabric length
points.text: 4 metres = 400 centimetres

example.problem: Did Priya finish shopping in time and stay in budget?
example.solution: Yes! She spent ₹450 (budget ₹500 ✓), has ₹50 left, and has 165 minutes to shop (plenty of time).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use time, money, and measurements together to plan a real shopping trip.

slides.title: The Race Home
slides.storyContext: Priya finishes shopping at 3:45 PM. That's 3 hours and 45 minutes before 5:00 PM — wait, that's wrong! She has 1 hour and 15 minutes to get home. She and Rohan hurry, buy snacks quickly, and leave the market by 4:30 PM. Safe!
slides.inSimpleWords: Always leave time for travel. Calculate carefully so you don't run late.

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan a School Picnic
slides.storyContext: You have ₹800 for a class picnic. Snacks cost ₹300, juice ₹250, and cups ₹100. The picnic is from 3:30 PM to 5:00 PM. How much money is left, and how long is the picnic?

points.label: Calculate spending
points.text: Add all costs

points.label: Find change
points.text: Subtract total cost from ₹800

points.label: Calculate time
points.text: From 3:30 PM to 5:00 PM

example.problem: Total cost = ₹300 + ₹250 + ₹100. Money left? Picnic duration?
example.solution: Total cost = ₹650. Money left = ₹800 − ₹650 = ₹150. Picnic time: 1 hour 30 minutes or 90 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use real shopping and time problems to practice your maths skills.

slides.title: Challenge: Measurement Puzzle
slides.storyContext: The fair booth is 5 metres long and 3 metres wide. Priya needs to measure the perimeter (edge all the way around) using her tape. How many metres of trim does she need to buy for the edges?

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: distance around the edge of a shape

points.label: Calculation
points.text: (5 + 3 + 5 + 3) metres = 16 metres

example.problem: Booth is 5m long and 3m wide. How much trim for all edges?
example.solution: Perimeter = 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 metres of trim.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add all the sides of a shape to find the perimeter.

slides.title: Challenge: Time Calculation with Travel
slides.storyContext: Priya needs to travel home, which takes 20 minutes. If she leaves the market at 4:30 PM, what time will she arrive home? Will she make it before 5:00 PM?

points.label: Travel time
points.text: 20 minutes

points.label: Arrival time
points.text: 4:30 PM + 20 minutes = 4:50 PM

example.problem: Leave at 4:30 PM, travel for 20 minutes. Arrive at what time?
example.solution: 4:30 PM + 20 minutes = 4:50 PM. Yes, before 5:00 PM!

slides.inSimpleWords: Add travel time to departure time to find arrival time.

slides.title: What We Learned Today
slides.storyContext: Priya's market adventure taught us three big maths ideas.

points.text: **Time:** Hour hand (short) and minute hand (long) tell us hours and minutes. Count minutes from one time to another. Special times: quarter past (15), half past (30), quarter to (45).
**Money:** Add up rupees to find total cost. Subtract from your budget to find change. Indian rupees: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 coins and ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100 notes. Always check for better deals.

**Measurement:** 1 metre = 100 centimetres = 1000 millimetres. Use measuring tapes to find lengths. Estimate for quick guesses, measure for exact answers. Perimeter is the edge distance around a shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Time, money, and measurement are maths tools we use every day to plan and budget our lives.

image.alt: What We Learned Today — Time, Money, Measurement

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Cricket Scorecard Adventure
hook: Track cricket runs with pictographs and bar graphs — see data tell the story of the match!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: cricket enthusiast keeping score

characters.name: Aisha
characters.role: data expert and cricket coach

characters.name: Dev
characters.role: team captain

slides.title: Data Handling
slides.storyContext: Arjun is recording data from a cricket match. He writes down runs scored by each player, then organizes the data into pictures and graphs to find out who played best!

image.alt: Data Handling — Data Handling

slides.title: The Class Cricket Match
slides.storyContext: Arjun's class team plays against the other class. Arjun is keeping score. Dev scored 12 runs, Aisha 10 runs, Rohan 8 runs, Priya 6 runs, and Arun 4 runs. Arjun writes down all the numbers, but there are too many to see at a glance. He asks Aisha how to show this data clearly so everyone can understand.
slides.inSimpleWords: Arjun has numbers but needs a clear way to show who scored the most runs.

image.alt: The Class Cricket Match — Data Handling

slides.title: What is Data? Collecting Information
slides.storyContext: Aisha explains: 'Data is information we collect. Like runs scored, heights of students, favorite fruits — anything we measure or count.'

points.label: Data
points.text: information collected by counting or measuring

points.label: Examples
points.text: scores, ages, rainfall, number of books read

points.label: Organizing
points.text: we write data in lists first, then show it in pictures or graphs

example.problem: Arjun wrote: Dev 12, Aisha 10, Rohan 8, Priya 6, Arun 4. Is this data?
example.solution: Yes! This is data — runs scored by each player, collected and written down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data is facts and numbers we collect to understand something.

image.alt: What is Data? Collecting Information — Data Handling

slides.title: Organizing the Scorecard
slides.storyContext: Arjun writes the data in a neat table: Player | Runs. Dev | 12. Aisha | 10. Rohan | 8. Priya | 6. Arun | 4. 'Good!' says Aisha. 'Now I can see all the numbers in one place. But a picture would be even clearer!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Tables organize data so you can read it easily. But pictures are even better!

slides.title: Making a Table: The First Step in Data Work
slides.storyContext: Before drawing any graph, create a neat table with titles and rows. This helps you organize and not miss any data.

points.label: Column headers
points.text: top row labels (e.g., 'Player' and 'Runs')

points.label: Data rows
points.text: each row has one data entry (Dev-12, Aisha-10, etc.)

points.label: Neat layout
points.text: lined up columns make reading easy

example.problem: Create a table for these runs: Dev 12, Aisha 10, Rohan 8, Priya 6, Arun 4.
example.solution: | Player | Runs | | Dev | 12 | | Aisha | 10 | | Rohan | 8 | | Priya | 6 | | Arun | 4 |

slides.inSimpleWords: Organize data in a table with labels and neat rows before making graphs.

slides.title: Pictographs: Using Pictures to Show Data
slides.storyContext: Aisha shows Arjun a pictograph. Each cricket bat symbol (🏏) stands for 2 runs. Dev scored 12 runs, so his row has 6 bat symbols. Rohan scored 8 runs, so his row has 4 bat symbols.

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: shows data using pictures or symbols

points.label: Symbol meaning
points.text: each symbol = a number (1, 2, 5, or 10)

points.label: Reading
points.text: count symbols in each row to find data for each person

example.problem: If 1 bat = 2 runs, how many bats for 12 runs?
example.solution: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 bats. Draw 6 bat symbols in Dev's row.

slides.inSimpleWords: A pictograph uses symbols (like bats or stars) to show numbers. Count the symbols to see the data.

slides.title: Arjun Draws the Pictograph
slides.storyContext: Arjun sits down with a pencil and draws cricket bats. Dev: 6 bats. Aisha: 5 bats. Rohan: 4 bats. Priya: 3 bats. Arun: 2 bats. 'Look at this!' he shows Aisha. 'I see right away Dev scored the most. I didn't have to read each number!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Drawing pictures of data makes it super easy to understand at a glance.

slides.title: Creating a Full Pictograph
slides.storyContext: Arjun needs to create a complete, labeled pictograph.

points.label: Title
points.text: 'Runs Scored in Match' at the top

points.label: Symbol rows
points.text: Dev: 🏏🏏🏏🏏🏏🏏 (6 bats = 12 runs)

points.label: Legend
points.text: '1 bat = 2 runs' so readers understand the symbol value

example.problem: Draw a pictograph for Dev 12 runs, Aisha 10 runs, Rohan 8 runs where 1 bat = 2 runs.
example.solution: Title: 'Match Runs'. Dev row: 🏏🏏🏏🏏🏏🏏. Aisha row: 🏏🏏🏏🏏🏏. Rohan row: 🏏🏏🏏🏏. Legend: 1🏏 = 2 runs.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complete pictograph has a title, symbol rows, and a legend explaining the symbol value.

slides.title: Building a Pictograph Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Aisha build a pictograph together. First, they list the data: Dev 12, Aisha 10, Rohan 8, Priya 6, Arun 4. Then they choose a symbol (cricket bat) and decide: 1 bat = 2 runs.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Collect and list the data (player names and runs)

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Choose a symbol and decide its value (e.g., 1 bat = 2 runs)

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Draw the symbol row for each player (Dev: 6 bats, Aisha: 5 bats, etc.)

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Add a title and label each row

example.problem: Show Arun's 4 runs using bats (1 bat = 2 runs).
example.solution: Arun gets 4 ÷ 2 = 2 bats in his row.

slides.inSimpleWords: A pictograph is easy to read: list your data, pick a symbol and its value, draw rows of symbols, and label everything.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Symbol
slides.storyContext: Aisha asks Arjun: 'What symbol represents cricket best?' Arjun picks a bat (🏏). But he could also pick a ball (⚫), a helmet (🪖), or a trophy (🏆). 'The best symbol matches the sport or data you're showing,' explains Aisha.
slides.inSimpleWords: Pick symbols that make sense for your data. A bat for cricket, an apple for fruit, etc.

slides.title: Bar Graphs: Comparing Data with Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Aisha now shows Arjun a bar graph. The bottom shows player names, the side shows a scale (0 to 12). Each player gets a tall or short bar showing their runs.

points.label: Bar graph
points.text: uses rectangles (bars) to show data

points.label: Horizontal axis
points.text: shows categories (player names)

points.label: Height of bar
points.text: matches the data value (Dev's bar is tall = 12 runs)

example.problem: In a bar graph, if Priya scored 6 runs, how tall is her bar?
example.solution: Her bar reaches the 6 mark on the vertical scale.

slides.inSimpleWords: A bar graph has a horizontal line at the bottom (showing names) and a vertical line on the side (showing numbers). Each bar's height shows the data.

slides.title: Drawing a Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws bars for each player. He uses a ruler to make them precise. Dev's bar reaches 12, Aisha's reaches 10, Rohan's reaches 8, Priya's reaches 6, Arun's reaches 4. 'Perfect!' says Aisha. 'Now you can compare at a glance.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use a ruler to draw precise bars. Taller bars = higher numbers.

slides.title: Steps to Draw a Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns the exact steps for creating a bar graph.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Draw two lines: horizontal (bottom) for categories, vertical (left) for scale

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Mark scale numbers (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) on vertical axis

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Write player names along horizontal axis

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Draw a bar for each player, height matching their runs. Use a ruler!

example.problem: Draw a bar graph for Dev 12, Aisha 10, Rohan 8.
example.solution: Dev's bar reaches 12, Aisha's reaches 10, Rohan's reaches 8. All bars start at 0 and go up.

slides.inSimpleWords: Build a bar graph step by step: axes, scale, names, then bars with correct heights.

slides.title: Reading a Bar Graph: Who Scored Most?
slides.storyContext: Looking at the bar graph, Arjun asks: 'Who has the tallest bar?' Aisha points to Dev — his bar reaches 12. 'That's the most runs. Now look at the shortest bar.' Arun's bar reaches 4.

points.label: Tallest bar
points.text: = highest data value (Dev 12 runs, most)

points.label: Shortest bar
points.text: = lowest data value (Arun 4 runs, least)

points.label: Comparing bars
points.text: see at a glance who did well and who didn't

example.problem: In the graph, whose bar reaches 10?
example.solution: Aisha's bar reaches 10 — she scored 10 runs.

slides.inSimpleWords: A bar graph lets you see and compare data instantly by looking at bar heights.

slides.title: Comparing Pictographs and Bar Graphs
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at both graphs. 'I like the pictograph because the bats are fun,' he says. 'I like the bar graph because it's more exact,' says Aisha. 'They both work! Use pictographs when you want to be fun and visual. Use bar graphs when you want exact numbers.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Pictographs are fun and easy to understand. Bar graphs are more precise and easier to compare exact values.

slides.title: Reading Data: Answering Questions
slides.storyContext: Aisha gives Arjun questions to answer using the graph: 'Who scored the most? How much more than the least? What's the total of the top two scorers?' Arjun reads the graph carefully: Dev 12 (most), Arun 4 (least), difference 8. Top two: Dev 12 + Aisha 10 = 22.

points.label: Find the maximum
points.text: tallest bar = highest value (Dev 12)

points.label: Find the minimum
points.text: shortest bar = lowest value (Arun 4)

points.label: Calculate differences
points.text: subtract to compare (12 − 4 = 8)

example.problem: How much more did Dev score than Arun?
example.solution: Dev 12 − Arun 4 = 8 more runs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs help you answer questions about data. Read carefully and do the math!

slides.title: Full Data Story: The Match Analysis
slides.storyContext: Arjun shows the coach both the pictograph (bats for 2 runs each) and the bar graph. The coach sees Dev was the top scorer and Arun needs practice. The data tells the whole story of the match.

points.label: Pictograph data
points.text: Dev: 6 bats, Aisha: 5 bats, Rohan: 4 bats, Priya: 3 bats, Arun: 2 bats (1 bat = 2 runs)

points.label: Bar graph data
points.text: Bars rise to 12, 10, 8, 6, 4 respectively

points.label: Story from data
points.text: Dev led the team; Arun needs more coaching

example.problem: Why is a pictograph and bar graph better than just a list of numbers?
example.solution: Both are visual — you see immediately who scored most without reading and comparing each number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pictures and graphs turn numbers into a story you can see and understand instantly.

image.alt: Full Data Story: The Match Analysis — Data Handling

slides.title: Make Your Own Pictograph: Favorite Fruits
slides.storyContext: In Arjun's class, 10 students like mangoes, 8 like bananas, 6 like apples, and 4 like oranges. Draw a pictograph using one apple symbol = 2 students. How many symbols for each fruit?

points.label: Mangoes
points.text: 10 students ÷ 2 = 5 symbols

points.label: Bananas
points.text: 8 students ÷ 2 = 4 symbols

points.label: Apples
points.text: 6 students ÷ 2 = 3 symbols

points.label: Oranges
points.text: 4 students ÷ 2 = 2 symbols

example.problem: Draw a pictograph with title 'Favorite Fruits' where 1 apple symbol = 2 students.
example.solution: Mangoes row: 5 apples, Bananas row: 4 apples, Apples row: 3 apples, Oranges row: 2 apples. Add a legend: 1 apple = 2 students.

slides.inSimpleWords: Take a list of numbers and turn it into a pictograph by dividing by the symbol value.

slides.title: Challenge: Draw a Bar Graph of Sports
slides.storyContext: Arjun surveys his friends: Cricket 8 students, Football 6, Badminton 5, Tennis 3. Draw a bar graph. Which sport is most popular? How many more students like cricket than tennis?

points.label: Scale
points.text: 0 to 10 on the vertical axis

points.label: Most popular
points.text: Cricket (8 students)

points.label: Difference
points.text: Cricket minus Tennis = 8 − 3 = 5 more students

example.problem: Bar graph of sports: Cricket 8, Football 6, Badminton 5, Tennis 3. Who won? Difference?
example.solution: Cricket is most popular (tallest bar). 8 − 3 = 5 more students like cricket than tennis.
