slides.inSimpleWords: Food takes a journey through your body for 6-8 hours. First mouth, then stomach, then intestines. Each stop breaks food down more.

slides.title: Proteins - Building and Repair
slides.storyContext: Farmer Uncle explains: 'I grow dal (lentils) and grow chickens for eggs. Both have protein to build strong bodies.'

points.label: What proteins do
points.text: Proteins build muscle, bone, hair, and skin. They repair cuts and bruises. They fight germs. They are the building blocks of your body.

points.label: Protein sources
points.text: Eggs, milk, yogurt, cheese, chicken, fish, meat, beans, lentils, peanuts, soy.

points.label: How much you need
points.text: Growing children (like you) need protein every day — at least at two meals — because your body is getting bigger and stronger.

example.problem: Why do mothers tell children to drink milk and eat eggs?
example.solution: Milk and eggs have lots of protein to build strong muscles. They also have calcium for growing bones and teeth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proteins are builders — they create strong muscles, bones, and skin, and fix damage when you get hurt.

image.alt: Proteins - Building and Repair — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Muscle Growth Story
slides.storyContext: Ananya notices her older brother getting stronger from playing cricket every day. 'Ananya, when I exercise, my muscles tear a tiny bit,' he explains. 'Protein fixes those tears and makes the muscle bigger. That's why athletes eat lots of eggs and chicken.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your muscles are like workers — they need protein to repair and grow stronger after playing or exercising.

slides.title: Fats - Energy and Warmth
slides.storyContext: Mummy heats oil in a pan and explains: 'A little bit of fat keeps you warm and stores energy inside your body.'

points.label: What fats do
points.text: Fats store lots of energy (more than carbohydrates). They keep you warm. They help your brain and skin stay healthy.

points.label: Healthy fats
points.text: Olive oil, peanut oil, ghee, coconut oil, nuts, fish oil, butter (in small amounts).

points.label: Balance matters
points.text: Some fat is needed and good. Too much fat makes you overweight and tired. The right amount gives slow, lasting energy.

example.problem: Why do we need fat but not too much?
example.solution: A little fat keeps organs warm and stores energy for long activities. Too much fat clogs arteries and makes the heart work too hard.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fats are long-burning fuel — your body stores them for energy during times of scarcity and to keep you warm.

image.alt: Fats - Energy and Warmth — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: The Winter Store
slides.storyContext: Farmer Uncle points at a layer of fat on his arms during winter. 'In summer, we work all day under the hot sun. Our body burns lots of energy. But in winter, we work less. That fat I stored in summer keeps me warm and gives me energy when food is scarce. Nature built us smart.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your body is smart — it stores fat like a savings account for energy, to be used when you need it most.

slides.title: Vitamins and Minerals - Health Guards
slides.storyContext: Ananya's mother piles colorful vegetables on a plate: orange carrots, green spinach, red tomatoes, yellow papaya. 'Each color brings different vitamins.'

points.label: Vitamins
points.text: Vitamin A (carrots, spinach) helps eyes see. Vitamin C (citrus, tomatoes) helps wounds heal and fights germs. Vitamin D (eggs, milk, sunlight) helps bones grow.

points.label: Minerals
points.text: Calcium (milk, yogurt, greens) builds strong bones and teeth. Iron (spinach, meat) makes blood carry oxygen. Iodine (salt) helps the brain.

points.label: Rainbow eating
points.text: Different colors = different nutrients. Eat red, orange, yellow, green, and purple foods every day to get all vitamins and minerals.

example.problem: Why does a child's teeth fall out and grow back, but an adult's don't?
example.solution: Children are still building bones and teeth, so they need lots of calcium and vitamin D. Adults' bones and teeth are done growing, so they need less.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vitamins and minerals are tiny bodyguards — they keep your eyes sharp, bones strong, blood healthy, and skin glowing.

image.alt: Vitamins and Minerals - Health Guards — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: The Rainbow Plate Game
slides.storyContext: Mummy challenges Ananya: 'Today, let's eat a rainbow! Red for vitamin C, orange for vitamin A, green for calcium and iron, yellow for energy.' Ananya picks tomato (red), carrot (orange), spinach (green), banana (yellow). By the end of the day, she feels amazing — no tiredness, clear eyes, strong legs.
slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbow eating is fun and powerful — when you eat many colors, your body gets all the vitamins and minerals it needs to stay healthy and strong.

slides.title: Vitamin Deficiency Story
slides.storyContext: Ananya's friend stopped eating fruits and vegetables. After weeks, he got tired and his teeth hurt. 'That's scurvy,' Mummy explains, 'from not eating vitamin C. Old sailors got this on long voyages without fresh food.'

example.problem: Why did sailors in the 1700s get scurvy on long ocean journeys?
example.solution: They ate only stored foods like bread and meat, no fresh fruits or vegetables. Vitamin C deficiency (from no citrus, greens) made their gums bleed and teeth fall out. Fresh limes or lemons prevented it — that's why British sailors ate limes (lime-juicers).

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body needs vitamins and minerals constantly. Skip them for weeks and your body breaks down — teeth hurt, wounds don't heal, you feel weak.

slides.title: Water - The Most Important
slides.storyContext: Mummy serves a glass of water to Ananya and says: 'Drink plenty. Your body is 70% water. It needs water to work.'

points.label: What water does
points.text: Water carries nutrients to every cell. It helps digest food. It cools you when you sweat. It carries waste out of your body.

points.label: How much to drink
points.text: Drink 6-8 glasses of plain water every day. More if you exercise or play sports. More if it's hot outside.

points.label: Water sources
points.text: Plain water, milk, juice, soup, and watery fruits (watermelon, orange) all count. Soda and sugary drinks are not healthy water.

example.problem: Why do athletes drink a lot of water during play?
example.solution: When you exercise, your body heats up and sweats to cool down. Sweat is water leaving your body. You must drink water to replace it or you dehydrate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is life — it flows through every part of your body to keep everything working smoothly and cool.

image.alt: Water - The Most Important — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: The Dry Garden
slides.storyContext: Ananya watches her mother forget to water plants one hot day. By evening, they wilt. Next morning, after watering, they perk up. 'Your body is like this plant,' Mummy says. 'Without water, even if you eat perfectly, your body gets tired and weak. Water brings everything to life.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your body is like a plant — without water, it wilts. With water, it thrives. Never forget to drink!

slides.title: A Balanced Plate
slides.storyContext: Mummy teaches Ananya to plan a healthy lunch: rice (carb), dal (protein), vegetables (vitamins), yogurt (protein and calcium), and water.

example.problem: Design a healthy lunch for a 10-year-old growing child.
example.solution: 1 cup rice or roti (carbohydrate for energy), 1 cup dal or chicken curry (protein for muscles), 2 bowls mixed vegetables (vitamins, minerals), 1 bowl yogurt (protein, calcium), 1 glass water. This gives all six nutrients in the right amounts.

slides.inSimpleWords: A healthy meal has a mix — grains for energy, protein to grow, colorful veggies for health, and water to keep everything flowing.

image.alt: A Balanced Plate — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Real Indian Breakfast Breakdown
slides.storyContext: Ananya eats idli with sambar and chutney for breakfast. Let's break down every nutrient.

example.problem: What nutrients are in a South Indian breakfast of idli with sambar and coconut chutney?
example.solution: Idli (steamed rice-lentil cake) = carbs + protein. Sambar (spiced vegetable stew) = vitamins, minerals, fiber. Coconut chutney = healthy fat + minerals. All three together = complete breakfast with energy, strength, health protection, and satisfaction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Traditional Indian meals are naturally balanced — rice for energy, dal for protein, vegetables for health, oil for warmth. Your grandparents knew nutrition before science proved it!

slides.title: Food as Medicine
slides.storyContext: When Ananya gets a cold, Mummy makes warm turmeric milk with ginger and honey. 'These aren't just delicious,' Mummy says, 'they have real medicine inside. Turmeric fights germs. Ginger helps your throat. Honey soothes cough. We've used these for thousands of years.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Some foods are medicine — they don't just feed you, they heal you. Garlic, turmeric, ginger, honey, and citrus all fight sickness naturally.

slides.title: Build Your Perfect Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: Ananya must plan breakfast, lunch, snack, and dinner using the nutrition rules she learned.

example.problem: You have 1 hour to play cricket. What should you eat before to have energy but not feel sick?
example.solution: A banana (carbs, easy to digest) or toast with jam (quick carbs) 30 minutes before. After play, eat protein like milk or paneer to repair muscles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eating right at the right time gives your body the energy to play, learn, and grow without crashes or sickness.

image.alt: Build Your Perfect Day of Eating — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Guess the Nutrient
slides.storyContext: Ananya plays a game with Mummy: guess which nutrients are hiding in everyday foods.

example.problem: In a glass of milk, name at least 4 nutrients and what each does.
example.solution: Carbs (lactose for quick energy), proteins (casein for muscle), calcium (strong bones), fat (vitamin D absorption and warmth), vitamins A & B (energy and vision). One glass has everything except fiber!

slides.inSimpleWords: Most foods are multitaskers — each food contains several nutrients working together to feed your whole body.

slides.title: The Festival Feast
slides.storyContext: On a festival day, Ananya's extended family gathers and cooks a huge meal. She sees variety: 'Why do we cook so many different dishes?' Grandma smiles: 'No single food has everything. We cook many things so everyone gets all six nutrients. Plus, variety keeps meals interesting and fun!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Eating a wide variety of foods ensures your body gets every nutrient it needs. Plus, variety tastes better and keeps meals exciting.

slides.title: Spot the Fake Health Food
slides.storyContext: Ananya sees cereal labeled 'fruit flavored' but it has no actual fruit, just sugar and color. She also sees whole grain bread and fresh fruit juice. Which is healthy? Which is a trick?

example.problem: Juice box labeled 'natural fruit juice' with orange color, vs. a fresh orange. Which is healthier?
example.solution: The fresh orange. Juice box has fiber removed and extra sugar added. Fresh orange has fiber, natural sugars, water, and vitamins intact. Labels trick you — read ingredients, not just labels.

slides.inSimpleWords: Just because packaging says 'healthy' or 'natural' doesn't mean it is. Always read the ingredient list — fresh and whole foods are always better than processed.

slides.title: Your Body is What You Eat
slides.storyContext: Ananya now knows that every bite is a choice to help her body grow strong, smart, and healthy.

points.text: Carbohydrates give quick energy to run, play, and think.
Proteins build muscles, bones, hair, and repair your body.
Fats give long-lasting energy and keep you warm.
Vitamins and minerals keep your eyes, bones, blood, and skin healthy.
Water is in every cell and makes everything work.
A balanced meal has all nutrients — eat the rainbow, stay strong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good nutrition is a superpower — eat well, and your body grows tall, strong, smart, and never gets tired.

image.alt: Your Body is What You Eat — Food and Nutrition

subject: Science
title: Karthik's Matter Lab
hook: Explore solids, liquids, and gases with Karthik as he plays with everyday items and discovers their secrets.

characters.name: Karthik
characters.role: curious scientist who questions everything around him

characters.name: Science Teacher Priya
characters.role: guides Karthik through hands-on experiments

characters.name: Sister Neha
characters.role: asks unexpected questions that reveal deeper truths

slides.title: Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases
slides.storyContext: Karthik wonders: 'Why is a rock hard but water is wet? Why can't I see air but I can feel wind?'

slides.title: Everything is Made of Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik's Science Teacher Priya sets up a simple lab at school with a rock, a glass of water, an air pump, and a balloon. 'Everything around you is made of matter,' she says. 'Let's see why solids, liquids, and gases behave so differently.'

slides.title: Karthik's Question Box
slides.storyContext: Karthik fills a box with items: a pencil, water, a balloon full of air, sand, milk, clay. He pokes each one and asks: 'Why does pencil say no, but water says yes? Why does the balloon push back?' Sister Neha says, 'That's because they're three different states of matter. Let's figure out the pattern.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Everything around you is made of tiny invisible pieces called atoms. How these atoms are packed together decides if something is solid, liquid, or gas.

slides.title: What is Matter?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya holds up a brick, a cup of water, and an empty balloon. 'All three are matter — everything that has mass and takes up space.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Matter is anything that has mass (weighs something) and volume (takes up space). Every object, liquid, and gas is matter.

points.label: Three states
points.text: Solid (keeps shape), liquid (flows but keeps volume), gas (spreads to fill any space).

points.label: Why they differ
points.text: The difference is how tightly the tiny bits (atoms and molecules) are packed together.

example.problem: Is air matter if you cannot see it?
example.solution: Yes — air has mass (a balloon full of air weighs more than an empty balloon). Air takes up space (it fills the balloon). So air is matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matter is anything you can feel, see, or weigh — rocks, water, air, paper, food — everything around you.

slides.title: Solids - Fixed Shape and Size
slides.storyContext: Karthik picks up a pencil, a book, a coin, and a wooden block. Sister Neha asks: 'What's the same about all these?'

points.label: What solids are
points.text: Solids have a fixed shape that doesn't change. They have a fixed volume — they don't shrink or grow. You can hold them.

points.label: Why solids are solid
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a solid are packed very tightly together, all holding hands in a rigid grid. They vibrate but stay in place.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Rock, wood, metal, plastic, bone, paper, ice, glass, cement.

example.problem: If you cut a wooden block in half, does it still behave like a solid?
example.solution: Yes — each half keeps its shape and volume. A solid's atoms are bound so tightly that breaking it doesn't change its state of matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solids are stubborn — they keep their shape and refuse to change, no matter how you move them around.

slides.title: The Marble Game
slides.storyContext: Karthik watches marbles roll across the floor, each one staying round and solid. 'They're all the same shape! They don't squish or stretch.' But when he tries to squeeze them with both hands, they don't budge. 'That's because atoms in a solid are holding hands tightly,' Teacher Priya explains, 'like a crowd where nobody can squeeze through.'
slides.inSimpleWords: In a solid, atoms are packed so tight they lock into a fixed shape — they're crowded, stuck, and strong.

slides.title: The Stretchy Solid Experiment
slides.storyContext: Karthik stretches a rubber band and watches it snap back. 'It's still solid, but it can change shape!' Teacher Priya explains: 'Some solids are flexible because their atoms can move a little before snapping back. Rubber is special — the atoms let it stretch but don't let it flow like liquid.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Some solids are flexible — rubber, sponges, springs. But they all snap back to their original shape because atoms stay packed together.

slides.title: Breaking a Solid
slides.storyContext: Karthik snaps a pencil in half. 'I broke it, but both pieces are still solid pencils! The atoms must be holding tight, even when the pencil breaks into pieces.' Sister Neha adds: 'That's because solid atoms are locked in a grid. When you break it, you don't change the state — you just make more solids from one solid.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Breaking or cutting a solid makes smaller solids, not liquids or gases. Atoms stay packed and locked even when the object breaks apart.

slides.title: Liquids - Flows but Keeps Volume
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya pours water into a tall glass, then pours the same water into a wide, flat plate. Karthik notices: 'The water changes shape!'

points.label: What liquids are
points.text: Liquids have no fixed shape — they flow and take the shape of their container. They have a fixed volume — you can measure 1 liter and it stays 1 liter.

points.label: Why liquids flow
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a liquid are loosely packed. They can slide past each other, so the liquid flows and changes shape.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Water, milk, oil, juice, honey, mercury (liquid metal), blood, petrol.

example.problem: You pour 1 liter of water into a tall thin glass, then into a short wide bowl. Has the volume changed?
example.solution: No — it's still 1 liter. The shape changed but the amount of water stayed the same. This is what makes liquids special.

slides.inSimpleWords: Liquids are flexible — they pour and change shape, but the total amount never changes.

image.alt: Liquids - Flows but Keeps Volume — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: The Sliding Dance
slides.storyContext: Karthik pours honey slowly and notices it flows differently than water. 'Honey moves slower,' he says. Teacher Priya nods: 'All liquids have loose atoms that can slide past each other. Honey's atoms are more tangled, so they slide more slowly. Water's atoms slide faster. But both flow and change shape — that's what makes them liquid.'
slides.inSimpleWords: In a liquid, atoms are loose enough to slide around each other — like a crowd where people can move and squeeze through, but the total crowd size stays the same.

slides.title: Gases - Fill Any Space
slides.storyContext: Karthik blows air into a balloon. The balloon expands and gets bigger. 'Where does all the air come from? The air is invisible!'

points.label: What gases are
points.text: Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume — they spread to fill any space they're in. A gas in a tiny bottle spreads to fill a huge room.

points.label: Why gases spread
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a gas are very far apart and move super fast. They bump into walls and each other, spreading everywhere.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Air, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor (steam), smoke, helium (balloons), natural gas, chlorine.

example.problem: You open a bottle of perfume in a room. Soon everyone smells it. Why?
example.solution: Perfume liquid evaporates into perfume gas. The gas molecules spread out, bump into air molecules, and travel through the entire room in minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gases are free spirits — they zoom around and spread to fill any space, no matter how big or small.

slides.title: The Perfume Mystery
slides.storyContext: Sister Neha opens a perfume bottle at one corner of the classroom. Within minutes, everyone at the other end smells it. 'How did it get here?' Karthik asks. Teacher Priya explains: 'Perfume atoms evaporate into gas. Gas atoms move super fast and spread everywhere, bumping into air. That's why you smell it even far away.'
slides.inSimpleWords: In a gas, atoms are so far apart and moving so fast they zoom around and spread to fill every corner of a space.

slides.title: The Balloon Pressure
slides.storyContext: Karthik inflates a balloon and it gets bigger and tighter. 'The air inside is pushing on the rubber!' Teacher Priya explains: 'Gas atoms move so fast they crash into walls constantly. Trillions of crashes per second create pressure — that's what keeps the balloon inflated.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Gas pressure is billions of atoms crashing into walls every second. That pressure pushes outward in all directions.

slides.title: Changing Between States
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya heats ice water over a burner. Karthik watches ice melt to water, then water boil into steam (gas). 'It's still the same stuff!'

points.label: Melting
points.text: Heating a solid breaks some bonds — atoms get loose and slide around. Ice (solid) melts to water (liquid) at 0°C.

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Heating a liquid gives atoms so much energy they break free. Water (liquid) evaporates to steam/vapor (gas) at 100°C.

points.label: Condensation and freezing
points.text: Cooling reverses it: steam condenses to water, water freezes to ice. Same matter, different state.

example.problem: Ice, water, and steam are all H2O. Why do they behave so differently?
example.solution: The amount of heat energy changes how tightly atoms hold together. Cold = tight grip (ice). Warm = loose slide (water). Hot = zooming free (steam).

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat is magic — it gives atoms energy to break free. Add heat, atoms spread apart (melting and evaporation). Remove heat, they huddle together (freezing and condensation).

slides.title: The Ice Cube Adventure
slides.storyContext: Karthik places an ice cube on a hot pan. It melts to water. The water gets hotter and starts to steam. 'Wait, the ice turned into water, then into invisible air? How is that possible?' Teacher Priya smiles: 'Same atoms, different arrangement. Heat rearranges them.'
slides.inSimpleWords: One substance can be solid, liquid, or gas — it all depends on temperature. Heat spreads atoms apart. Cold pushes them together.

slides.title: Dry Ice Magic
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya shows dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) to Karthik. When she leaves it at room temperature, it doesn't melt to liquid — it turns straight into gas! 'It's skipping the liquid stage,' Neha observes. Teacher Priya explains: 'That's called sublimation. Some solids can jump directly to gas when they get warm.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Some solids skip the liquid stage and go straight to gas when heated. Dry ice, mothballs, and some salts do this — it's called sublimation.

slides.title: Properties of Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik and Neha test different materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, water, air. They measure hardness, weight, flexibility, and transparency.

points.label: Physical properties
points.text: Shape, size, color, hardness, flexibility, density (heavy or light), solubility (dissolves in water), transparency (see-through).

points.label: Density
points.text: How much mass fits in a certain volume. Lead is dense (heavy and small). Foam is light (lots of space, little mass).

points.label: Solubility
points.text: Some solids dissolve in water (sugar, salt). Some don't (sand, stone). Gases dissolve too (oxygen, CO2).

example.problem: Sugar dissolves in water to become invisible. Is it still matter?
example.solution: Yes — the sugar atoms are still there, mixed between water molecules. You can taste them and heat the water to evaporate it and get the sugar back.

slides.inSimpleWords: Properties are the fingerprints of matter — color, hardness, weight, how it dissolves, what it looks like.

image.alt: Properties of Matter — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: The Heavy vs. Light Game
slides.storyContext: Karthik picks up a ball of lead (small, heavy) and a big ball of foam (big, light). 'These are different sizes but different weights! Why?' Sister Neha explains: 'Density is how tightly atoms are packed. Lead atoms are packed super tight — small but heavy. Foam atoms are spread out — big but light.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Density is how squished together atoms are. Tight atoms = dense and heavy. Spread-out atoms = light and fluffy.

slides.title: Everyday Matter Changes
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya lists things Karthik sees every day and asks him to identify the state changes.

example.problem: What state changes happen when you cook rice?
example.solution: Solid rice grains → water boils (liquid to gas) → steam rises → rice absorbs liquid water → rice becomes softer but still mostly solid. Multiple changes in one process.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cooking, laundry, weather, and breathing all involve matter changing states — melting, evaporating, freezing, condensing.

slides.title: Boiling Eggs Science
slides.storyContext: Karthik boils an egg and watches the shell crack. 'The solid egg white turned rubbery. Why did boiling change it?' Teacher Priya explains: 'Heat reorganized the protein atoms. Heat doesn't always cause state changes — it can also change properties.'

example.problem: An egg white is liquid before boiling but solid after. Did it change state or just change properties?
example.solution: It changed properties, not state. The egg white's liquid proteins got heat energy and bonded differently, becoming solid. It's not melting/freezing/evaporating — it's a chemical change, not just a physical state change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat can do two things: change the state of matter (solid to liquid) or change properties (liquid to rubbery solid). Both involve heat!

slides.title: The Sinking and Floating Mystery
slides.storyContext: Karthik puts iron and wood in water. Iron sinks, wood floats. 'They're both solids, but they act different!' Sister Neha explains: 'It's about density. Iron atoms are packed tighter than iron's weight displaced water. Wood atoms are loose enough that the water pushes it up.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Denser objects sink (iron), less dense objects float (wood, ice). It's all about whether atoms are packed tighter or looser than water.

slides.title: Sort the Matter Mystery Box
slides.storyContext: Sister Neha puts items in a box: a stone, honey, air, milk, ice, sugar, smoke, oil. Karthik must sort them by state and explain each choice.

example.problem: Air is invisible. How do you know it's a gas and not nothing?
example.solution: Air has mass (a balloon filled with air weighs more than empty). Air takes up space (it fills the balloon and pushes the balloon walls outward). Therefore, air is matter in the gas state.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every material fits into one of three states based on whether it has fixed shape, fixed volume, and how it flows or spreads.

image.alt: Sort the Matter Mystery Box — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: Design the Perfect Container
slides.storyContext: Karthik must design a container for: (1) a solid pencil, (2) liquid milk, (3) a gas balloon. Each needs a different strategy.

example.problem: Why does milk need a lid but a pencil doesn't, even though both are in containers?
example.solution: A pencil is solid — it keeps its shape and won't escape. Milk is liquid — it flows and needs a container to hold its shape. A gas (balloon air) needs an airtight, elastic container because it spreads to fill any space.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different states need different containers — solid needs support, liquid needs a boundary, gas needs a seal that won't burst.

slides.title: State Change Prediction
slides.storyContext: Karthik must predict: if I heat snow, what happens? If I cool steam, what happens? If I heat liquid mercury?

example.problem: Predict the state changes: You start with ice and keep adding heat for 10 hours. What do you get?
example.solution: Ice (solid) → water (liquid) at 0°C → steam (gas) at 100°C → superheated steam (hotter gas) at higher temps. After 10 hours of continuous heating over a fire, you'd have very hot steam or even plasma.

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat makes matter move from solid to liquid to gas. If you remove heat, it goes backward: gas to liquid to solid.

slides.title: Three States, One Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik now sees that matter is everywhere — rocks, water, air — and each behaves according to its state.

points.text: Matter is anything with mass and volume — everything around you.
Solids keep a fixed shape and volume — atoms are packed tightly.
Liquids flow and take container shape but keep volume — atoms can slide.
Gases spread to fill any space — atoms zoom around freely.
Heat energy changes states: melting, evaporation, condensation, freezing.
Every material has properties: color, hardness, density, whether it dissolves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ice, water, and steam are the same matter in three forms — temperature is the magician that changes them.

image.alt: Three States, One Matter — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

subject: Science
title: Divya's Sky Diary
hook: Follow Divya as she explores rain, wind, clouds, and seasons — and learns why weather changes.

characters.name: Divya
characters.role: observes clouds and rain in her village

characters.name: Grandpa Hari
characters.role: a farmer who reads the sky and seasons

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Divya's friend who records weather daily

slides.title: Weather and Climate
slides.storyContext: Divya watches dark clouds gather in the sky. 'Grandpa, why does the sky change? When will it rain?'

slides.title: Reading the Sky
slides.storyContext: On a hot afternoon in June, Divya sits with Grandpa Hari in their village field. He points at the western horizon where dark clouds are building. 'Every year the monsoon rains come,' he says. 'The sun heats the ocean, water rises, and the clouds release rain. Let me teach you how this works.'

slides.title: The Sky Watcher's Notebook
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Divya start a notebook to record weather every morning: temperature, cloud type, wind speed, humidity, and rain. After a week, they notice patterns. 'Look!' Ravi points. 'Every time those dark clouds appear, it rains the next day. Grandpa's knowledge is pattern recognition!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Farmers and weather watchers learn by observing patterns over time — today's clouds predict tomorrow's weather.

slides.title: What is Weather?
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Divya note the temperature, clouds, wind, and rain in their notebook every morning for a week.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Weather is the condition of the air right now — hot, cold, rainy, windy, cloudy. Weather changes day to day.

points.label: Weather elements
points.text: Temperature (hot or cold), humidity (wetness in air), wind (moving air), rain, sunshine, clouds.

points.label: Climate
points.text: Climate is the average weather of a place over many years. India's climate is tropical (hot and rainy in monsoon, hot in summer, cool in winter).

example.problem: Today it rained and tomorrow it will be sunny. Is the climate changing?
example.solution: No — weather changed from rainy to sunny. Climate changes only over decades, not days. Climate is the pattern; weather is today's surprise.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather is what happens today. Climate is the pattern of weather over years. Weather makes you carry an umbrella; climate makes a place dry or wet overall.

image.alt: What is Weather? — Weather and Climate

slides.title: The Weather vs. Climate Debate
slides.storyContext: Ravi says 'Look, it's so hot today — the climate is getting hotter!' Grandpa Hari shakes his head. 'One hot day is weather. You track weather for 30 years, then we talk climate. Last year was also hot this time. Ten years before that, it was hotter. That's the real pattern — climate.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Don't confuse one rainy day with the rainy season, or one hot day with global warming. Climate is the long-term pattern, not today's surprise.

slides.title: The Water Cycle - Rain's Journey
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari traces the path of water: 'Evaporation lifts water into the sky. Condensation makes clouds. Precipitation brings rain back to Earth.'

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Heat from the sun turns water (oceans, rivers, lakes, soil) into invisible water vapor. The vapor rises into the sky.

points.label: Condensation
points.text: High in the sky, it's cold. Water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets. Millions of droplets form a cloud.

points.label: Precipitation
points.text: When droplets in a cloud get heavy enough, they fall as rain (or snow in cold places, or sleet, or hail).

points.label: Collection
points.text: Rain falls into oceans, rivers, lakes, and soil. The cycle starts again.

example.problem: A puddle disappears on a sunny day even though it doesn't rain. Where does the water go?
example.solution: Heat from the sun causes evaporation. The water turns into water vapor and rises into the sky. You can't see it, but it's there heading toward the clouds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water travels in a circle — the sun heats it to vapor (evaporation), it rises and cools to droplets (condensation), drops as rain (precipitation), and the sun heats it again.

image.alt: The Water Cycle - Rain's Journey — Weather and Climate

slides.title: The Puddle Vanishing Act
slides.storyContext: Divya watches a puddle disappear after rain. 'Grandpa, where did the water go? Is it gone forever?' Grandpa Hari smiles: 'Watch the ocean when the sun heats it. Heat pulls water up, up, up into the sky where it cools and falls as rain again. That puddle is on an adventure — it will come back as clouds and rain.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Water is recycled forever — it evaporates into the sky, condenses into clouds, falls as rain, and starts again. Nothing is wasted.

slides.title: The Breath of Earth
slides.storyContext: Divya watches steam rise from boiling water and realizes: 'That's evaporation happening in front of me! The water turned invisible and floated up.' Grandpa Hari adds: 'Every plant, every lake, every ocean does this constantly. The whole Earth breathes — water up, water down, water up again.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Evaporation happens everywhere — puddles, oceans, leaves, soil. Billions of tons of water evaporate daily and fall as rain somewhere else.

slides.title: Clouds - Made of Water Droplets
slides.storyContext: Ravi points at the sky. 'Different clouds mean different weather. Divya, can you tell which will rain?'

points.label: What clouds are
points.text: Clouds are billions of tiny water droplets (or ice crystals in cold air) floating together. They form when water vapor condenses high in the atmosphere.

points.label: Cloud types
points.text: Cumulus (white, puffy, fair weather), stratus (flat, gray, low), cirrus (wispy, high, icy), nimbus (dark, brings rain or thunderstorms).

points.label: Cloud height
points.text: Height affects weather. Low clouds = rain or drizzle. High clouds = fair weather. Dark clouds = heavy rain coming.

example.problem: Why are clouds white but the sky is blue?
example.solution: Water droplets scatter all colors of light equally — that looks white to us. Clear air lets blue light scatter more — that looks blue.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clouds are floating water — billions of droplets stuck together, invisible until they condense and show as white or gray shapes in the sky.

slides.title: Cloud Watching
slides.storyContext: Divya lies on the grass watching clouds change shape. 'Ravi, look! That cloud looks like a buffalo! But it keeps changing.' Grandpa Hari nods: 'Clouds are moving, spreading, merging. By watching them, you learn to predict weather — dark clouds that grow fast mean rain is coming.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Clouds are not solid — they're always moving and changing. By watching cloud shapes and colors, you predict tomorrow's weather.

slides.title: The Anvil Cloud Warning
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari suddenly points at a tall cloud shaped like an anvil. 'See that flat top? That's a thunderstorm anvil. When you see that, get indoors. The storm will be here in 30 minutes with hail, lightning, and strong winds.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Cloud shapes tell stories — anvil clouds mean thunderstorms, wispy clouds mean fair weather, dark towers mean heavy rain coming soon.

slides.title: Wind - Moving Air
slides.storyContext: A strong breeze shakes the trees. Grandpa Hari explains: 'Wind is air moving. Why does air move? Because the sun heats Earth unevenly.'

points.label: What causes wind
points.text: The sun heats land and water unevenly. Warm air over the ocean rises. Cool air over land sinks. Moving air between them = wind.

points.label: Local vs. global winds
points.text: Sea breeze (daytime, ocean to land). Land breeze (nighttime, land to ocean). Trade winds and monsoon winds are large patterns.

points.label: Monsoon
points.text: India's monsoon is a seasonal wind shift. In June-September, winds blow from the ocean and bring heavy rain. This is India's main rainy season.

example.problem: Why does it always get windy just before heavy rain arrives?
example.solution: Heavy rain clouds are pushed by strong winds. The wind speeds up as it brings the clouds closer. When clouds arrive, wind and rain come together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wind is air on the move — the sun heats things unevenly and pushes the air around, creating breezes and storms.

slides.title: The Sea Breeze Secret
slides.storyContext: Divya visits the coast and notices: during the day, wind blows from ocean to land (sea breeze). At night, it reverses (land breeze). 'Why?' she asks. Grandpa Hari explains: 'Land heats and cools faster than water. Hot air rises, cool air sinks. The sun makes the dance, and air follows.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The sun doesn't heat everything equally — it heats land faster than ocean. This creates wind as air moves from hot to cold places.

slides.title: The Monsoon Prediction
slides.storyContext: Divya tracks the monsoon's arrival. In May, winds come from the north (hot, dry). In early June, she feels the shift — winds now blow from the southwest over the ocean. 'The monsoon has switched!' Grandpa Hari confirms. 'In two weeks, those wet winds will bring rain.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Seasons change when winds shift direction. The monsoon is a massive seasonal wind reversal that brings rain to half the world.

slides.title: Temperature - Hot and Cold
slides.storyContext: Divya checks a thermometer every morning and evening for a month. 'Why is it hotter at noon than at sunrise? Why are nights cooler than days?'

points.label: Day and night
points.text: The sun is high in the sky at noon — lots of rays hit Earth → hot. At sunrise and sunset, sun is low — rays spread out → cool. At night, no sun → coldest.

points.label: Seasons
points.text: Earth tilts. In summer, India tilts toward the sun → very hot. In winter, India tilts away → cool. Spring and fall are in between.

points.label: Ocean effect
points.text: Coastal cities are cooler in summer (ocean absorbs heat) and warmer in winter (ocean releases heat). Inland cities are hotter in summer, colder in winter.

example.problem: India is hot in May and June. Why is it even hotter just before monsoon rain arrives?
example.solution: Summer heat builds up. Air over land and ocean gets very hot and humidity rises (lots of water vapor). Clouds form but haven't released rain yet. The air is hot and sticky.

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature depends on the sun's angle, the season, and whether you're near water — the whole Earth is constantly tilted and spinning, so temperature changes constantly.

slides.title: The Tilt and Seasons
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws Earth tilted on his notebook. 'In June, India leans toward the sun — super hot! In December, India leans away — cool!' Divya sees it: the tilt changes how directly the sun hits, and that changes temperature. 'So Earth is always tilted the same way, but it spins around the sun?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Earth tilts as it orbits the sun. When your part tilts toward the sun, it's summer (hot). When it tilts away, it's winter (cool).

slides.title: Seasons in India
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari points at the calendar. 'See how the year divides? Each season brings different weather and affects our crops.'

points.label: Summer (March-May)
points.text: Very hot, especially in May-June. Dry winds. Temperature can reach 45°C in North India. People drink lots of water, use fans and shade.

points.label: Monsoon (June-September)
points.text: Heavy rain, winds, and cooler temperatures. The southwest monsoon brings 80% of India's yearly rainfall. Farmers plant crops now.

points.label: Fall/Autumn (October-November)
points.text: Rains decrease. Temperature drops. Clear skies. Crops mature and are harvested. Pleasant weather for outdoor work.

points.label: Winter (December-February)
points.text: Cool and dry, especially in North India (10-15°C). South India stays warmer (20-25°C). Clear skies, less rain. Winter crops grow.

example.problem: Why do farmers plant seeds just as the monsoon rains arrive?
example.solution: They know from generations of watching the sky: June rains = soil moisture → seeds can germinate and grow. Planting now means crops are ready to harvest by October-November.

slides.inSimpleWords: India has four seasons with different temperatures, rain, and winds — each season is perfect for certain crops and activities.

slides.title: The Farmer's Calendar
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari teaches Divya the farmer's year: 'In May, heat kills crops. June rain starts. July-September, we water from rain. October, harvest. December-February, winter crops. February-May, heat returns. Repeat. Nature gives rhythm; we follow.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every season has a purpose for farmers — summer heats, monsoon waters, fall harvests, winter regrows. Nature's rhythm guides when to plant and when to harvest.

slides.title: Reading the Weather Like Grandpa
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari teaches Divya to predict weather by watching the sky, wind, and clouds — like farmers have done for thousands of years.

example.problem: Grandpa says: 'If the evening sky is red, tomorrow will be fair. If the morning sky is red, rain is coming.' Is this science or superstition?
example.solution: This is science. Red sky = dust particles in the air. Evening red = dust from today still in air = fair tomorrow. Morning red = dust from a distant storm coming = rain coming soon. Grandpa's rule works because he's observing atmospheric particles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Farmers have watched weather patterns for millennia — they read clouds, wind, temperature, and animal behavior to predict rain and seasons.

slides.title: Humidity and Comfort
slides.storyContext: Divya notices that on some hot days she feels sticky and tired, while on others she feels light and energetic even though the temperature is the same. 'Humidity,' Grandpa explains, 'is how much water vapor is in the air. High humidity means sweat can't evaporate, so you feel trapped by heat.'

example.problem: Two days are both 35°C, but one feels much hotter. Why?
example.solution: Humidity. Day 1 has high humidity (lots of water vapor), so sweat can't evaporate and you feel trapped. Day 2 has low humidity (dry air), so sweat evaporates fast and cools your body. Same temperature, different feel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Humidity is the water vapor in the air. High humidity = sticky and uncomfortable. Low humidity = dry and breezy. Temperature alone doesn't tell the whole story.

slides.title: Dew and Frost Formation
slides.storyContext: Divya wakes early and sees grass covered in dew (water droplets). 'How did water appear on the grass if it didn't rain?' Grandpa Hari explains: 'During the night, the ground cooled. The water vapor in the air cooled too and condensed into droplets — same as clouds, but on the ground. It's called dew. If it's really cold, it becomes frost.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Dew is water vapor condensing on cold grass at night. Frost is the same thing, but frozen. Both form when the temperature drops enough to cool the air.

slides.title: Hail and Sleet Mystery
slides.storyContext: During a winter storm, Divya sees ice pellets falling — sometimes clear balls of ice (hail), sometimes layers of ice (sleet). Grandpa Hari explains: 'In thunderstorms, rain gets blown up into freezing air, freezes solid, falls, gets blown up again, freezes more — creating layers of ice ball. Sleet is rain that freezes as it falls. Both happen when the upper air is ice-cold.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Hail is rain that freezes in the freezing air of thunderstorms. Sleet is rain that freezes while falling. Both need cold upper air to form.

slides.title: Predict the Weather
slides.storyContext: Divya keeps a weather diary for two weeks. She notes temperature, clouds, wind, humidity, and rain. At the end, can she predict what weather is coming?

example.problem: You see dark nimbus clouds, strong winds from the west, and humidity rising. What will happen next?
example.solution: Heavy rain will arrive within hours. Clouds are full of water. Wind is bringing them closer. High humidity means lots of water vapor. These are all signs of an imminent thunderstorm.

slides.inSimpleWords: By watching temperature, clouds, wind, and humidity together, you can predict weather like a real meteorologist.

image.alt: Predict the Weather — Weather and Climate

slides.title: Weather Records Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Divya track weather for a month and answer: What's the hottest day? The rainiest day? The windiest? Which season is coming based on trends?

example.problem: Your weather records show temperature rising, humidity rising, clouds increasing. What season is coming?
example.solution: Summer is ending and monsoon is coming. Rising heat and humidity = air getting warmer and wetter. Increasing clouds = water vapor condensing. Rain is imminent (within days to weeks).

slides.inSimpleWords: By tracking weather patterns over weeks and months, you learn to predict which season is arriving and when to expect major changes.

slides.title: Compare Climates
slides.storyContext: Divya learns that deserts are dry, rainforests are wet, and mountains are cold. She wonders: 'If weather changes daily, how do climates stay so different?'

example.problem: A desert gets only 10cm rain per year, while a rainforest gets 250cm. Why such a huge difference?
example.solution: It's geography. Deserts sit where winds don't bring moisture. Rainforests sit where winds blow over oceans year-round, creating constant rain. Climate is determined by latitude, ocean currents, mountains, and wind patterns — all permanent features.

slides.inSimpleWords: Climate is locked in place by geography — mountain valleys stay cold, oceans near the equator stay warm, and deserts stay dry because that's how the Earth is shaped.

slides.title: Earth's Air and Water Dance
slides.storyContext: Divya now understands that weather and climate are driven by the sun, water, and air in constant motion.

points.text: Weather is today's air conditions — temperature, clouds, rain, wind.
Climate is the average weather pattern of a place over years.
The water cycle moves water: evaporation (rises) → condensation (clouds) → precipitation (rain) → collection (repeats).
Clouds form when water vapor cools and condenses. Different clouds bring different weather.
Wind is air moving because the sun heats Earth unevenly. Monsoons are seasonal winds with heavy rain.
India has four distinct seasons with different temperatures, rain, and winds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather and climate are nature's rhythm — the sun heats, water rises, air moves, clouds form, and rain falls in an endless dance that shapes life on Earth.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Big Mela Shop Adventure
hook: Arjun counts toys at the village fair and discovers how big numbers help us read price tags.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: curious student who loves solving number puzzles

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Arjun's clever friend who notices patterns in numbers

slides.title: The Big Toy Shop
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya visit a mela (fair) with a toy shop. The shopkeeper says there are 3,247 toys in the store!

points.label: Setting
points.text: A busy village fair in Delhi with colourful toy stalls

slides.inSimpleWords: Arjun sees a HUGE number at the toy shop.

image.alt: The Big Toy Shop — Numbers up to 10000

slides.title: Place Value: Thousands
slides.storyContext: The shopkeeper explains: 3,247 means 3 thousands, 2 hundreds, 4 tens, and 7 ones. Priya draws it out.

points.label: 3 thousands
points.text: 3,000 — three full bags of 1,000 toys each

points.label: 2 hundreds
points.text: 200 — two boxes of 100 toys

points.label: 4 tens
points.text: 40 — four bundles of 10

points.label: 7 ones
points.text: 7 — single toys

slides.inSimpleWords: Each digit holds a different place value.

image.alt: Place Value: Thousands — Numbers up to 10000

slides.title: Breaking Down a Price
slides.storyContext: A remote-control car costs ₹5,432. Arjun wants to write it in words and in parts.

example.problem: Write 5,432 in expanded form and in words.
example.solution: 5,432 = 5,000 + 400 + 30 + 2 = Five thousand, four hundred thirty-two

slides.inSimpleWords: Split the number by its place values.

image.alt: Breaking Down a Price — Numbers up to 10000

slides.title: Comparing Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya notices the doll collection has 2,890 dolls and the action figure stall has 3,150. Which is bigger?

points.label: Odd numbers
points.text: End in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 — always have one leftover

slides.title: Comparing Odd and Even Across Range
slides.storyContext: Priya explores patterns: between 1,000 and 2,000, how many numbers end in odd vs. even digits?

slides.title: Estimating with Rounded Numbers

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya Discovers the Ancient Library
hook: Priya reads book numbers written as I, V, X and learns a 2,000-year-old number system.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: helps Priya decode the mystery of old number marks

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: discovers Roman numerals on ancient library shelves

slides.title: The Old Library Mystery
slides.storyContext: Priya visits her grandmother's library and finds books marked VI, XII, VIII. She wonders why they don't use normal numbers.

points.label: Setting
points.text: An old Delhi library with ancient books and dusty shelves

slides.inSimpleWords: Priya finds mysterious symbols on book spines.

image.alt: The Old Library Mystery — Roman Numerals

slides.title: The Basic Roman Symbols
slides.storyContext: Grandmother explains the five main symbols used for 2,000 years by Romans and still used today.

points.label: I
points.text: means 1 — like one finger

points.label: V
points.text: means 5 — like an open hand

points.label: X
points.text: means 10 — like two hands crossed

points.label: L
points.text: means 50 — an ancient Roman shape

points.label: C
points.text: means 100 — from the word 'Centum' (hundred)

slides.inSimpleWords: Five symbols build all Roman numbers.

image.alt: The Basic Roman Symbols — Roman Numerals

slides.title: Reading Simple Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arjun points to a book marked IVIII (4) and another marked VII (7). Priya counts the sticks.

example.problem: Read these Roman numbers: III | VI | VIII

slides.inSimpleWords: Add symbols from left to right.

image.alt: Reading Simple Numbers — Roman Numerals

slides.title: The Subtraction Rule
slides.storyContext: Grandmother shows a special trick: IV (4) doesn't mean 6; it means 5 minus 1 because I comes before V!

points.label: IV = 4
points.text: I (1) before V (5) means subtract: 5−1=4

points.label: IX = 9
points.text: I (1) before X (10) means subtract: 10−1=9

points.label: XL = 40
points.text: X (10) before L (50) means subtract: 50−10=40

points.label: XC = 90
points.text: X (10) before C (100) means subtract: 100−10=90

slides.inSimpleWords: A smaller symbol before a bigger one means subtract.

image.alt: The Subtraction Rule — Roman Numerals

slides.title: Subtraction in Action
slides.storyContext: Priya reads Volume IV (4) and Volume IX (9) from a series. She writes out both using subtraction.

example.problem: Decode: IV | IX | XL

slides.inSimpleWords: Smaller left of bigger means minus.

image.alt: Subtraction in Action — Roman Numerals

slides.title: Writing Numbers Up to 100
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns that XII is 10+1+1=12, and XIX is 10+(10−1)=19. Priya writes her age, 14, as XIV.
slides.inSimpleWords: Combine addition and subtraction rules.

image.alt: Writing Numbers Up to 100 — Roman Numerals

slides.title: Mixed Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Priya reads complex volumes: XVII (17), XLII (42), LXVIII (68). She breaks each one down.

example.problem: Decode: XVII | XLII | LXVIII

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply both rules in one number.

slides.title: Mystery Book Dates
slides.storyContext: The library books have publication years written in Roman numerals. One book is MDCCCXVII. Priya breaks it down.

points.label: Problem
points.text: M=1000, D=500, C=100. What year is MDCCCXVII?

example.problem: Decode MDCCCXVII

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn M (1000) and D (500) for bigger years.

image.alt: Mystery Book Dates — Roman Numerals

slides.title: The Larger Roman Symbols
slides.storyContext: Grandmother reveals that Romans didn't stop at C. They had D (500) and M (1000) for really big years and dates.

points.label: D
points.text: means 500 — Roman symbol for five hundred

points.label: M
points.text: means 1000 — from the word 'Mille' (thousand)

points.label: CD = 400
points.text: C before D: 500−100=400

slides.inSimpleWords: Two more symbols extend Roman numbers to 3,000+.

slides.title: Reading Old Building Dates
slides.storyContext: Priya sees a building corner stone marked MCMXVIII. She decodes the year the building was constructed.

example.problem: Read MCMXVIII (a building construction year)

slides.inSimpleWords: Decode centuries-old dates from monuments.

slides.title: Conversion: Roman to Modern (Hindu-Arabic)
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to translate ancient Roman numerals into the numbers we use today: 1, 2, 3, etc.

points.label: Two systems
points.text: Roman numerals (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) vs. modern (1, 2, 3, ...)

points.label: Same value
points.text: VII = 7, XLIV = 44, CCC = 300

points.label: Why modern?
points.text: Easier for math, place value, and large numbers

points.label: When to use Roman?
points.text: Formal dates, book chapters, clocks, movie credits

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip between old and new number styles.

slides.title: Conversion Practice
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a reference sheet. She lists book volumes and their modern equivalents to help younger students.

example.problem: Convert to modern: Volume I | Volume V | Volume X | Volume L
example.solution: Volume 1, Volume 5, Volume 10, Volume 50

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice switching between number systems.

slides.title: Rules of Roman Numeral Writing
slides.storyContext: Priya learns the official rules: only subtract one symbol from the next larger, and never repeat a symbol more than 3 times.

points.label: Only certain pairs subtract
points.text: I before V or X; X before L or C; C before D or M

points.label: No repeats > 3 times
points.text: Write IIII as IV; never IIII (except on clocks)

points.label: Example
points.text: 49 = XLIX (40=XL, 9=IX), not IL (wrong)

points.label: Order matters
points.text: Biggest to smallest, left to right

slides.inSimpleWords: Roman numerals follow strict rules.

slides.title: Writing Roman Numerals Correctly
slides.storyContext: Arjun practices writing years. He checks: is 1994 MCMXCIV or MIMXCIV? He applies the rules.

example.problem: Write in Roman numerals: 49 | 94 | 994
example.solution: 49 = XLIX; 94 = XCIV; 994 = CMXCIV

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the subtraction and order rules.

slides.title: The Clock Face Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Priya notices that clock faces mix Roman numerals in unusual ways. Some show IIII instead of IV for 4. Why might this be?

points.label: Observation
points.text: Some clocks use IIII (four I's) instead of IV (subtraction)

points.label: Question
points.text: Why would clockmakers avoid the subtraction rule?

example.problem: Ancient clocks often showed 4 as IIII. Write the full clock face (I through XII) this way.
example.solution: I, II, III, IIII, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII (symmetry and visual balance)

slides.inSimpleWords: Understand that rules can bend for design.

slides.title: The Roman Numerals Are Everywhere!
slides.storyContext: Walking home, Arjun spots Roman numerals on a clock, on monument stones, and even on school buildings. Priya realizes they're timeless.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: Clock faces, movie titles, building plaques, book volumes

slides.inSimpleWords: Roman numerals live in our modern world.

slides.title: Number Patterns in Roman Numerals
slides.storyContext: Arjun spots patterns: all odd-numbered years end in odd Roman numerals (I, III, V, VII, IX). Even years end in even shapes.

points.label: Odd years
points.text: End in I, III, V, VII, IX (1, 3, 5, 7, 9)

points.label: Even years
points.text: End in II, IV, VI, VIII, X (2, 4, 6, 8, 10)

points.label: Example
points.text: MCMXVII (1917) ends in VII (odd). MCMXVIII (1918) ends in VIII (even).

slides.inSimpleWords: Roman numerals follow the same odd/even patterns.

slides.title: Identifying Odd/Even in Roman Years
slides.storyContext: Priya catalogs old book dates and labels them by parity. Books from odd years go on the left shelf.

example.problem: Which year is odd: MDCCCLXVII or MDCCCLXVIII?
example.solution: MDCCCLXVII = 1867 (ends in VII = 7 = odd). MDCCCLXVIII = 1868 (ends in VIII = 8 = even).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the last symbol to spot odd or even.

slides.title: The Ancient Date Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Two old monuments have inscribed dates: MDCLXXV and MDCLXXVI. One is an odd year, one is even. Can Arjun sort them without converting?

points.label: Problem
points.text: Which is odd, which is even: MDCLXXV and MDCLXXVI?

example.problem: Classify without converting: MDCLXXV and MDCLXXVI
example.solution: MDCLXXV ends in V (5=odd year, 1675). MDCLXXVI ends in VI (6=even year, 1676).

slides.inSimpleWords: Classify Roman numerals without full conversion.

slides.title: Comparing Roman Numerals
slides.storyContext: Priya compares book volumes: Volume XIV vs. Volume XV. Which is bigger? She uses symbols, not conversion.

points.label: Visual method
points.text: More symbols usually means bigger number

points.label: XIV vs XV
points.text: Both have 3 symbols, but XV is bigger (15 vs 14)

points.label: XCIX vs C
points.text: XCIX has 4 symbols but C is bigger (100 > 99)

points.label: Key
points.text: Look at the largest symbol's value first

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare Roman numerals by their largest symbol.

slides.title: Ordering Roman Volumes
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges library volumes in order: IX, VII, XII, XXI, XV. He doesn't convert, just looks at symbols.

example.problem: Order from smallest to largest: IX | VII | XII | XXI | XV

slides.inSimpleWords: Arrange Roman numerals in sequence.

slides.title: Finding Missing Digits in Roman Numerals
slides.storyContext: An old book has a torn volume number: X_VIII. Priya knows it's between 17 and 19. What's the missing symbol?

points.label: Clue
points.text: The number is between XVII (17) and XIX (19)

points.label: Logic
points.text: X_VIII must equal 18, so the blank is V+II = V...no wait, VIII is only 8

points.label: Solution
points.text: It's XVI + II = XVIII (18), so X, V, I, I, I

slides.inSimpleWords: Use context clues to find missing Roman symbols.

slides.title: Decoding Damaged Dates
slides.storyContext: A stone carving shows: MDC_C_XVI. The underscores are worn away. What year is it?

example.problem: What's the year MDC_C_XVI if it's between 1800-1900?

slides.inSimpleWords: Reconstruct damaged Roman numerals from context.

slides.title: Priya Becomes the Library Expert
slides.storyContext: Priya offers to organize the library's ancient section. She writes a guide explaining Roman numerals to all visitors, from simple (I–X) to complex (MCMXCIX).

points.label: Legacy
points.text: An ancient number system still speaks to modern readers

slides.inSimpleWords: Knowledge of the past helps us understand today.

slides.title: Roman Numeral Recap
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun summarize their adventure through centuries of numbers.

points.label: Addition
points.text: Add symbols left to right

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: Smaller left of bigger = subtract

points.label: Real use
points.text: Clocks, books, dates, monuments

slides.inSimpleWords: Ancient Romans gave us a clever number code.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Cricket Ball Factory
hook: Arjun groups cricket balls to prepare for a tournament and learns multiplication and division shortcuts.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: runs a cricket ball factory and learns fast counting

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: organizes teams and shares balls fairly

slides.title: The School Tournament
slides.storyContext: The school cricket tournament is starting! Arjun's job is to prepare 6 boxes, each with 8 cricket balls. Priya helps organize.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: How many balls total? Counting one by one takes too long!

slides.inSimpleWords: Arjun needs a faster way to count groups.

image.alt: The School Tournament — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition
slides.storyContext: Instead of adding 8+8+8+8+8+8, Priya shows Arjun a shortcut: 6 times 8 = 6 × 8.

points.label: Shortcut
points.text: 6 × 8 = 48 (multiply instead of add)

points.label: Fast!
points.text: One multiplication beats six additions

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply to count equal groups quickly.

image.alt: Multiplication as Repeated Addition — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Multiplying by Groups
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees his factory has 4 warehouses with 7 boxes each. How many boxes total?

example.problem: 4 warehouses × 7 boxes each = ? boxes

slides.inSimpleWords: Groups × items per group = total items.

image.alt: Multiplying by Groups — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Division as Sharing Equally
slides.storyContext: Now 48 balls must be shared equally among 6 cricket teams. Priya divides: 48 ÷ 6 = how many per team?

points.label: Total
points.text: 48 balls

points.label: Teams
points.text: 6 teams

points.label: Each team gets
points.text: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 balls

points.label: Check
points.text: 6 × 8 = 48 ✓ (opposite operations)

slides.inSimpleWords: Division splits a big group into equal parts.

image.alt: Division as Sharing Equally — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Division in Action
slides.storyContext: A factory machine makes 36 cricket bats. Arjun packs them into 9 sets (one per team). How many bats per set?

example.problem: 36 bats ÷ 9 sets = ? bats per set
example.solution: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 bats per set. Check: 9 × 4 = 36 ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Share the total fairly into groups.

image.alt: Division in Action — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Multiplication Tables (Up to 10 × 10)
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Arjun the 3, 4, 5, 6 times tables so he can multiply without counting fingers.

points.label: Know them by heart
points.text: Speeds up all maths and problem-solving

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize key multiplication facts.

image.alt: Multiplication Tables (Up to 10 × 10) — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Using Times Tables
slides.storyContext: Arjun needs to find 7 × 8 quickly. He recalls the 7 times table: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56.

example.problem: Use the 7 times table to find: 7 × 3 | 7 × 6 | 7 × 8

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply multiplication tables to speed up solving.

slides.title: The Mixed-Up Order
slides.storyContext: A delivery truck brings 120 new cricket balls. Arjun must pack them into bags of 8 or 10. How many full bags each way? Are there leftovers?

points.label: Problem
points.text: 120 ÷ 8 = ? and 120 ÷ 10 = ? (Which leaves no remainder?)

example.problem: Divide 120 balls: into bags of 8 OR bags of 10?
example.solution: 120 ÷ 8 = 15 bags (no R). 120 ÷ 10 = 12 bags (no R). Both work!

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if numbers divide evenly.

image.alt: The Mixed-Up Order — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: The Inverse: Multiplication and Division Undo Each Other
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices: if 6 × 8 = 48, then 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 48 ÷ 8 = 6. They're opposites!

points.label: Multiplication creates groups
points.text: 6 × 8 = 48 (make 6 groups of 8)

points.label: Division breaks groups
points.text: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 (split 48 into 6 equal parts)

points.label: Inverse operations
points.text: Multiply then divide = return to the original

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply and divide are paired opposites.

slides.title: Using Inverse Operations to Verify
slides.storyContext: Priya double-checks Arjun's packing by working backwards. She divides the total and multiplies to confirm.

example.problem: Arjun says 7 boxes have 9 balls each (63 total). Verify by dividing.
example.solution: 63 ÷ 9 = 7. Yes, it checks out. (Or 63 ÷ 7 = 9.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use division to verify multiplication answers.

slides.title: Remainders: When Division Doesn't Split Evenly
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 25 balls and wants 6 equal piles. Each pile gets 4, but 1 ball is left over. That leftover is a remainder.

points.label: Division with remainder
points.text: 25 ÷ 6 = 4 remainder 1 (written 25 ÷ 6 = 4 R1)

points.label: What this means
points.text: 6 × 4 = 24, so 25 − 24 = 1 ball remaining

points.label: Remainders matter
points.text: In sharing, leftovers affect the final answer

slides.inSimpleWords: Some divisions leave a leftover piece.

slides.title: Dividing with Remainders
slides.storyContext: The tournament has 45 cricket fans but only 7 rows of benches with 6 seats each. Are there leftover fans without seats?

example.problem: 45 fans ÷ 7 rows = ? per row, remainder?
example.solution: 7 × 6 = 42, so 45 ÷ 7 = 6 R3. Three fans don't fit in the organized rows.

slides.inSimpleWords: Account for leftovers in real situations.

slides.title: Properties of Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Priya discovers shortcuts: 5 × 8 gives the same answer as 8 × 5 (both 40). Order doesn't matter!

points.label: Commutative
points.text: 3 × 7 = 7 × 3 = 21 (order doesn't matter)

points.label: Associative
points.text: (2 × 3) × 5 = 2 × (3 × 5) = 30 (grouping doesn't matter)

points.label: Identity
points.text: Any number × 1 = itself (6 × 1 = 6)

points.label: Zero
points.text: Any number × 0 = 0 (9 × 0 = 0)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication has handy shortcuts and rules.

slides.title: Using Multiplication Properties
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates boxes of balls. He uses properties to make it easier: 4 × 25 is hard, but 25 × 4 = 100 is easier.

example.problem: Solve using properties: (2 × 9) × 5 and 5 × (2 × 9)
example.solution: Both equal 90. (Associative property: grouping doesn't change the answer.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Rearrange to make multiplication easier.

slides.title: Tournament Day Success
slides.storyContext: The tournament begins. All 6 teams have exactly 8 cricket balls each. Arjun's factory is a success, and he never counted one by one!

points.label: Victory
points.text: Multiplication and division saved time and solved perfectly

slides.inSimpleWords: Smart maths solved the real-world challenge.

image.alt: Tournament Day Success — Multiplication and Division

slides.title: Odd and Even in Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers: even × anything = even. Odd × odd = odd. Odd × even = even. No exceptions!

points.label: Even × anything
points.text: Always even (2×5=10, 4×7=28)

points.label: Odd × even
points.text: Always even (3×4=12, 7×6=42)

points.label: Rule
points.text: One even factor makes the product even

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication follows strict odd/even rules.

slides.title: Predicting Products
slides.storyContext: Priya predicts whether a multiplication result will be odd or even before calculating.

example.problem: Is the result odd or even: 3×5 | 4×6 | 7×8 | 9×3
example.solution: Odd (15). Even (24). Even (56). Odd (27).

slides.inSimpleWords: Predict odd/even before multiplying.

slides.title: The Uneven Factor Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees a problem: ? × 6 = 72. Is the missing number odd or even? He doesn't need to solve it fully!

points.label: Problem
points.text: Is the unknown factor odd or even in: ? × 6 = 72

example.problem: Determine odd/even: ? × 6 = 72 (don't find answer, just parity)
example.solution: 72÷6=12 (even). The unknown is even. (Even÷even=even possible)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use parity rules to narrow down possibilities.

slides.title: Multiplication Patterns (Times 9, 11, 5)
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun clever patterns: all 9 multiples have digits that sum to 9. All 5 multiples end in 0 or 5.

points.label: Times 5
points.text: Always ends in 0 or 5 (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30)

points.label: Times 11
points.text: Pattern repeats the digit (11, 22, 33, 44, 55)

points.label: Time-saver
points.text: Use patterns to check if multiplication is correct

slides.inSimpleWords: Spot patterns in times tables.

slides.title: Checking Answers with Patterns
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates 9 × 47 = 423 and checks using digit-sum: 4+2+3 = 9, so it's correct!

example.problem: Check if correct using patterns: 5 × 32 = 160 | 9 × 56 = 504
example.solution: 160 ends in 0 ✓ (5 multiple). 504: 5+0+4=9 ✓ (9 multiple).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use number patterns to verify multiplication.

slides.title: Division with Money
slides.storyContext: Arjun divides the tournament prize pool: ₹720 equally among 8 winning teams. Each team gets ₹90.

points.label: Problem
points.text: ₹720 ÷ 8 teams = ? per team

points.label: Solution
points.text: 720 ÷ 8 = 90 (each team gets ₹90)

points.label: Real-world
points.text: Division happens with money, supplies, rewards

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide money fairly among groups.

slides.title: Sharing Prize Money
slides.storyContext: The cricket tournament has three cash prizes: ₹2,400 (first), ₹1,800 (second), ₹1,200 (third). Each must split equally among team members.

example.problem: If first-place team has 6 players, each gets: 2,400 ÷ 6 = ?
example.solution: 2,400 ÷ 6 = 400. Each player gets ₹400.

slides.inSimpleWords: Split prizes and money fairly.

slides.title: Word Problems with Multiplication/Division
slides.storyContext: Real-world problems mix both operations: start with groups, then split or combine. Arjun learns to spot the operation needed.

points.label: Multiply when
points.text: You have equal groups and count the total

points.label: Divide when
points.text: You have a total and split into equal groups

points.label: Read carefully
points.text: Look for clues: 'total', 'each', 'share', 'groups'

points.label: Check answer
points.text: Use the opposite operation to verify

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify when to multiply or divide.

slides.title: Solving Mixed Word Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya reads: 'The tournament organizer bought 9 crates of cricket balls, 12 balls per crate. They shared all balls equally among 6 teams. How many per team?'

example.problem: 9 crates × 12 balls = ? total. Then total ÷ 6 teams = ? per team
example.solution: 9 × 12 = 108 balls total. 108 ÷ 6 = 18 balls per team.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve step-by-step using both operations.

slides.title: The Young Mathematician's Reputation
slides.storyContext: By tournament's end, Arjun becomes known as the 'number wizard' of school. Coaches ask for his help organizing teams and equipment.

points.label: Recognition
points.text: Multiplication and division skills open doors to leadership

slides.inSimpleWords: Math skills earn respect and real-world responsibility.

slides.title: Multiplication & Division Mastered
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya celebrate their mastery of these powerful shortcuts.

points.label: Multiply
points.text: Count equal groups fast

points.label: Divide
points.text: Share fairly into groups

points.label: Opposites
points.text: Multiply and divide undo each other

points.label: Tables
points.text: Know times facts to solve instantly

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication and division are speedy math superpowers.

image.alt: Multiplication & Division Mastered — Multiplication and Division

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Chocolate Cake Party
hook: Priya bakes a cake, cuts it into pieces, and learns fractions and decimals by sharing with friends.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: bakes cakes and discovers fractions through sharing

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: helps measure recipe ingredients and split portions

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Bake
slides.storyContext: Priya bakes a big chocolate cake for her birthday. She cuts it into 8 equal slices. Arjun eats 2 slices. What fraction did he eat?

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake, 8 equal pieces, Arjun takes 2 pieces

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of something whole.

image.alt: The Birthday Cake Bake — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: the bottom number (8) tells you how many equal parts. The top number (2) tells you how many parts Arjun got.

points.label: Numerator (top)
points.text: 2 — the pieces Arjun got

points.label: Denominator (bottom)
points.text: 8 — total equal slices

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 2/8 (two-eighths) of the cake

slides.inSimpleWords: Top = parts taken, bottom = total parts.

image.alt: Understanding Fractions — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions in Real Cakes
slides.storyContext: Priya cuts another cake into halves (2 parts). Arjun eats 1 half. She cuts a third cake into quarters (4 parts) and Arjun gets 1 quarter.

example.problem: Name the fractions: 1 half, 1 quarter, 2 halves
example.solution: 1/2 (one-half), 1/4 (one-quarter), 2/2 = 1 whole (two halves)

slides.inSimpleWords: Halves, thirds, quarters are common fractions.

image.alt: Fractions in Real Cakes — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 1/4 cake left. Arjun has 1/2 cake left. Who has more?

points.label: Same numerators
points.text: 1/4 vs 1/2 — smaller denominator = bigger piece
Half is bigger than a quarter

points.label: Tip
points.text: Smaller bottom number = bigger actual piece

slides.inSimpleWords: Smaller bottom means a bigger slice.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Intro to Decimals
slides.storyContext: Arjun measures milk for the frosting: 0.5 litres (half a litre) and 0.25 litres (a quarter). Decimals use points, not fractions!

points.label: Decimal point
points.text: The dot (.) separates whole from parts
Same as 1/2 (five-tenths)
Same as 1/4 (twenty-five hundredths)
One-tenth of a whole
One-hundredth of a whole

slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals show parts using a point.

image.alt: Intro to Decimals — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions and Decimals Together
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a recipe: 3/4 cup sugar (same as 0.75 cup). She uses 1/2 cup flour (same as 0.5 cup). Arjun writes both ways.

example.problem: Write as both fraction and decimal: 3/4, 1/2, 1/10

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals are two ways to say the same part.

image.alt: Fractions and Decimals Together — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: The Cake Sharing Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya bakes 3 cakes. Each has 8 slices. She gives 2/8 to Arjun, 3/8 to a friend, and keeps 1/8. How many slices are left unsold?

points.label: Problem
points.text: Total 24 slices. 2/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 6/8. How many remain?

example.problem: 24 slices − (2/8 + 3/8 + 1/8) = ? slices left

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions and subtract from the total.

image.alt: The Cake Sharing Problem — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: The Party Success
slides.storyContext: Priya's birthday party is perfect. Everyone gets a fair share: Arjun gets 1/4, friend gets 1/3, family gets the rest. Fractions made sharing fair and fun!

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Fractions and decimals help us divide, measure, and share wisely in everyday life

slides.inSimpleWords: Fair sharing needs fractions and decimals.

image.alt: The Party Success — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions & Decimals Recap
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun recap their delicious discovery.

points.label: Fractions
points.text: Top = parts taken, bottom = total parts (e.g., 2/8)

points.label: Common fractions
points.text: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 3/4 appear everywhere

points.label: Decimals
points.text: Use a point: 0.5, 0.25, 0.75 = same as fractions

points.label: Use it
points.text: Cooking, measuring, sharing, money

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals split whole things fairly.

image.alt: Fractions & Decimals Recap — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: 2/8 cake is the same as 1/4 cake! Same piece, different names. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: 2/8 = 1/4 (both are half of a half)

points.label: How to make
points.text: Multiply or divide numerator AND denominator by the same number

points.label: Example
points.text: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 = 8/16 (all the same piece)

points.label: Simplify
points.text: 6/9 = 2/3 (divide both by 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: Same piece, different numbers = equivalent fractions.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 1/4 cake. Her friend brings 1/4 cake. Together, how much do they have? Arjun uses the same denominator trick.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add or subtract fractions with the same bottom number easily.

slides.title: Priya's Recipe Scaling
slides.storyContext: Priya wants to make 2 cakes instead of 1. The recipe says 1/2 cup sugar. For 2 cakes, she needs 1/2 × 2 = 1 cup. Multiplying fractions!

points.label: Scenario
points.text: Double the recipe, double each ingredient

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions to scale recipes up or down.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: To multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom. To divide: flip the second fraction and multiply.

points.label: Divide
points.text: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2 (flip the second fraction)

points.label: Real use
points.text: 3/4 × 2 = 6/4 = 1.5 cups (recipe scaling)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply tops and bottoms; flip to divide.

slides.title: Decimals in Measurement
slides.storyContext: Priya measures: 2.5 litres of milk, 0.75 grams of salt, 1.25 kg of flour. Understanding decimal place values helps her read scales accurately.

example.problem: What is 2.5 in fractions? And 0.75?
